doc.name: blog
doc.summary: List blog posts, or read one, from the published RSS feed.
doc.description: Reads the design system blog the same way any feed reader does, over the published RSS feed, never the blog's source files. With no slug it lists every post parsed from the feed; with a slug it reads that post's full plaintext body via the .txt alternate the feed advertises. Both envelopes carry feedUrl so a caller can hit the RSS feed directly.

params.name: slug
params.description: Post slug (matched case-insensitively) to read in full. Omit to list every post.

returns.description: The feed URL plus every post parsed from the feed, each with slug, title, description, date, type, authors, link, and its plaintext URL.
One post's metadata plus the feed URL and the post's full plaintext body.

throws.when: the slug is provided but is not a string
no post in the feed matches the requested slug
the RSS feed or post text cannot be fetched (network error, timeout, non-2xx, or oversized), or the post has no plaintext alternate in the feed

doc.name: build
doc.summary: Page-building assistant: the how-to-build playbook, or the page template to start from for an idea.
doc.description: The "build a page" entry point. Called with no query it returns the how-to-build-a-page playbook as data: the workflow steps with their commands, the on-system rules, and related lookups. Called with a query it names the page template to START from (always one: the page template a ranker built for long descriptions puts first; for a part of a page, the page it names; else the app shell) and the next two templates, and the unified search grouped around it: the other close page templates, drop-in blocks, and idea-specific components/hooks, plus the always-on frame + foundation. A template carries the page frame and spacing, so the kit never recommends composing a page from components.
doc.signature: build(query?: string, options?: BuildOptions): Promise<BuildHelpResponse | BuildKitResponse>

params.name: query
params.description: What you're building (e.g. "analytics dashboard"). Omit for the how-to-build playbook.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to resolve @astryxdesign/core and templates from.

params.name: options.type
params.description: Restrict the underlying search to a single domain.

params.name: options.limit
params.description: Max results pulled from search before grouping into the kit.

returns.description: Emitted when the query is omitted: the page-building playbook — `playbook: true`, a `title`, the ordered `steps` (each a `title`, its `commands`, and optionally what the step `returns`), the on-system `rules`, and `related` lookups. Each command is a bare subcommand ({command, purpose?}) for the caller to render with its own CLI invocation.

The page template to start from and the kit around it: the echoed query, hasResults/matchCount/directMatch fields, `start` (the template to scaffold, the `template <id> --type page <path>` command that selects it, whether the page ranker's pick is also search's direct match, the closest page, or the fallback app shell, the ranker's next two `alternatives`, and optional `notes` — setup notes naming what the template needs that the project lacks, such as missing packages or a missing StyleX compiler), search's closest page templates (≤3), drop-in block patterns (≤5), idea-specific components/hooks (≤6), and the always-on frame + foundation component-name arrays. Carries `hint` only when the kit came back thin — what to try instead, so a caller does not read a near-empty kit as "the package has nothing".

throws.when: a query is given and options.type is not a known domain, or options.limit is not a positive integer
a query is given and @astryxdesign/core cannot be found from cwd

a query is given outside a project, or in a project with nothing installed, and the Core of the release that answers is not beside it or cached, and cannot be installed into the per-user cache (offline, a registry without it, or an unwritable cache)

examples.label: Find the template to start from
examples.code:
const {data} = await build('analytics dashboard');
// data.start.command: 'astryx template dashboard --type page <path>'

doc.name: component
doc.summary: Resolve one or several components by name, or list the catalog, with optional focused slices (props, source, showcase, blocks).
doc.description: Routes on its arguments: one string resolves that component across core and integration packages; an array returns one ordered result row per selector at every array length; and no name returns the catalog grouped by category. Boolean flags narrow each resolved component to just its props, source, showcase, or example blocks. An integration component that replaces a Core component (its doc sets replaces, and its package declares the CLI range that turns replacement on) answers to the Core name in detail, batch, and list results; use options.package '@astryxdesign/core' for the original. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, components from integrations installed next to this CLI package globally resolve too; inside a project, only the project's own integrations count. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-integrations}.
doc.signature: component(name?: string | string[], options?: ComponentOptions): Promise<ComponentListResponse | ComponentBatchResponse | ComponentDetailResponse | ComponentDetailPropsResponse | ComponentDetailSourceResponse | ComponentDetailShowcaseResponse | ComponentDetailBlocksResponse>

params.name: name
params.description: Pass one selector string for the existing single-result response, or an array of at most 100 selectors for an ordered component.batch response. The limit counts duplicates in every projection mode. An array always requests a batch, including [] and ['Button']. Use 'Button', 'widgets/Button', '@acme/widgets/Button', or '@acme/widgets@1.2.3/Button'. A version applies to the package and must match the installed version. Omit the argument to list the catalog.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to resolve @astryxdesign/core from.

params.name: options.list
params.description: Return the grouped catalog instead of a single component.

params.name: options.category
params.description: List only the components in this group: a key of the unfiltered list (each component's group field), such as 'Layout' or 'Button'. It is not the category field of a component detail.

params.name: options.package
params.description: Scope lookup to a specific external package (e.g. '@acme/widgets'). Use '@astryxdesign/core' to select an original replaced by an integration component.

params.name: options.props
params.description: Return only the component's props table.

params.name: options.source
params.description: Return the component's source file.

params.name: options.showcase
params.description: Return the component's showcase example.

params.name: options.blocks
params.description: Return the component's example blocks (showcase, examples, related).

params.name: options.detail
params.description: Detail level for list views.
params.default: 'full' for a named component; 'brief' for lists (returned as data.detail: 'names')

params.name: options.lang
params.description: Language code for localized doc content: 'en', 'zh', or 'dense'.

params.name: options.zh
params.description: Shorthand for Chinese (zh) doc content.

params.name: options.dense
params.description: Return the token-efficient dense doc variant.

returns.description: The catalog grouped by component group. data.detail is the level ('names' | 'compact' | 'full') and data.components is the grouped map: names entries with name, package, and an optional canonical import for integration and legacy package components; brief entries; or full ComponentDoc entries.

An explicit selector array returns one ordered receipt at every array length: count and one results row per selector, including duplicates. ComponentBatchResponse specializes the shared BatchResponse and BatchRow types. Each row carries selector and status (found, not_found, ambiguous, or error); found rows carry the single-selector result, ambiguous rows carry installed candidates ({package, component, kind, installed}), and failed rows carry code, error, and optional suggestions.

One component's authored ComponentDoc plus ownership metadata (owner package, import specifier, whether source is available). When the name is a sub-component documented in a parent's doc, the payload is scoped to it and parentDoc names that parent.
Just the component's props table (ComponentPropDoc[]).
The component's source file, as {component, source}.
The component's showcase example, as {component, aspectRatio, source}.
The component's example blocks, as {component, showcase, examples, related} of BlockEntry.

throws.when: a selector array has more than 100 entries, a package-shaped selector has no component item, or its package conflicts with options.package
options.detail is not 'full', 'compact', or 'brief'
options.lang is set to anything other than 'en', 'zh', or 'dense'
@astryxdesign/core cannot be resolved from cwd

outside a project, or in a project with nothing installed, the Core of the release that answers is not beside it or cached, and cannot be installed into the per-user cache (offline, a registry without it, or an unwritable cache)
options.category is not a string or matches no component group
name is not a string, resolves to no known component, or is absent from the requested options.package
the component is provided by multiple packages (pass options.package to disambiguate)
options.package names a legacy external package that cannot be found, or a package-qualified selector requests a version that is not installed
the resolved component has no .doc.mjs typed doc file
the resolved component's .doc.mjs fails to load or validate
options.source is set but the component has no source file
options.showcase is set but the component has no showcase

doc.name: discover
doc.summary: Browse and search integrations: the ones a project has and, through the official list and discover sources, the ones it could add.
doc.description: Lists the integrations a project loads and the official packages it declares, then the packages it could add: the official Astryx packages first, from the list the CLI carries, then whatever the discover sources of the project and its integrations list, with what each one adds per kind. An @scope/name query shows one package with every version its source knows; @scope/name@version shows one version; @scope/name/Component returns an installed component's validated doc, and any other item path returns that item. A free-text term searches every item and package. Discover only reads: it prints the command that adds a package and never runs it. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, integrations installed next to this CLI package globally are listed as installed; inside a project, only the project's own are, and the compatible global ones are listed in `meta.available` with source `installed for this computer` and an `install` command. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-integrations}.
doc.signature: discover(query?: string, options?: DiscoverOptions): Promise<DiscoverListResponse | DiscoverDetailResponse | DiscoverDetailDocResponse | DiscoverItemResponse | DiscoverSearchResponse>

params.name: query
params.description: A package (@scope/name, optionally @version), an item path (@scope/name/<item>), or a free-text term. Omit to list packages.

params.name: options.components
params.description: In the CLI package list, print every component, and every other item, of each package instead of the first 10. A display flag for the CLI renderer; the programmatic response is unchanged.

params.name: options.type
params.description: Only one kind: in the list, packages that add it; in a search, items of that kind.

params.name: options.installed
params.description: Only what the project has. Cannot be set with options.available.

params.name: options.available
params.description: Only what the project could add. Cannot be set with options.installed.

params.name: options.limit
params.description: Max number of search results, a positive integer.

params.name: options.lang
params.description: Language code to translate a resolved component doc into.

params.name: options.zh
params.description: Return a resolved component doc in Chinese.

returns.description: What the project has: the integrations it loads and the official packages it declares (package, the npm package and always equal to name; name, category, components, version, and a list per other kind they add), official packages first. meta.available lists what the project could add, official packages first, each with its package and the command that adds it; inside a project, an integration installed for the computer that the project does not install is listed there too, with source `installed for this computer` and the install command for the project in `install`. meta.sources reports each source, the official list last. When it lists no integration it carries meta.configured.

One package: its package (the npm package the result is about), what the shown version adds, whether the project has it, its versions and latest release when a source knows them, and the command that adds it when the project does not have it. An entry from the official list lists the newest release this CLI knows as latest and the project's Core version; its add command pins the project's Core version, else the Core range it declares (quoted), else the latest release. A version or item the official list does not show answers ERR_UNKNOWN_PACKAGE.
The validated ComponentDoc for one installed component, for an @scope/name/Component query, plus package, the npm package that owns the component.
One item that is not an installed component: its kind, name, the package and version that add it, and whether the project has the package. The envelope's package names the same package.

The query echoed back plus every matching item and package, each with its kind and whether the project has it, even when one name matches exactly or only one item matches; total is set when the limit cut the list.

throws.when: the query is a non-string value, or a free-text search is run with an empty query
options.type is not a known kind, options.limit is not a positive integer, or options.installed and options.available are both set
neither the project, the official list, nor any discover source has the package
the item is not in the named package
a free-text term matches nothing, or the requested version is not published
the resolved component's docs fail to load or are malformed

doc.name: docs
doc.summary: Read the reference docs: list every topic, one topic's sections, one section, or a whole topic.
doc.description: No topic lists every reference-doc topic; a topic returns its whole ReferenceDoc, and `index: true` returns its section index (each section's key, title, and summary); a topic plus a section returns that one section. Token-ref blocks are inlined in every read, and so is a section's reference block: the doc it includes, then the command that opens that doc. The topic set is the CLI's own docs plus the ones the project's configured integrations contribute, including any topic an integration replaces or extends, so it depends on the cwd. A route opens a node of the docs tree instead: a namespace such as `cli/api` returns its children one level down (`depth` reads as many levels as asked, and `detail` how much of each doc below), a typed doc such as `cli/api/functions/search` returns its content, and a guide the tree places (`authoring/quick-start`) reads like any topic. Every read but the list carries `links`, the commands that move from it: `up` to the level it sits in, `previous` and `next` to its neighbors, and, for a typed doc, `related` to the docs it names (its command or function, and its related docs); `previous` and `next` to the section or node before and after it. Overlay options select localized or dense variants. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, doc topics from integrations installed next to this CLI package globally are listed too; inside a project, only the project's own integrations count. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-integrations}.
doc.signature: docs(topic?: string, section?: string, options?: DocsOptions): Promise<DocsListResponse | DocsIndexResponse | DocsDetailResponse | DocsDetailSectionResponse | DocsNodeResponse>

params.name: topic
params.description: Doc topic to load (e.g. 'principles'), a docs-tree route (e.g. 'cli/api/functions/search'), or the name of one node of the docs tree: its own name (e.g. 'tokens-color'), or its route without the prefix its name repeats (e.g. 'tokens/color'), where exactly one node answers to it. Omit to list all topics.

params.name: section
params.description: Section to return: its key (from the topic's index), its title, or a unique part of its title (case-insensitive).

params.name: options.lang
params.description: Language code for localized doc content.

params.name: options.zh
params.description: Shorthand for Chinese (zh) doc content.

params.name: options.dense
params.description: Return the token-efficient dense doc variant. It is written to be read whole, so it returns the whole doc.

params.name: options.index
params.description: Return the topic's section index (each section's key, title, and summary), even for a topic with one section.

params.name: options.depth
params.description: How many levels below a docs-tree namespace to read: 0 for the namespace alone, 1 for its children (the default), 'all' for every level. Where a read stops, a child with docs below it carries childCount. A doc with nothing below it reads the same at any depth. On the topic list, where each namespace otherwise lists alone, it names the docs below each one, as deep as asked; without it the list is unchanged.

params.name: options.detail
params.description: How much of each doc below the named one a depth read returns: brief (the default) is its identity; compact and full add its text (a guide's sections, a namespace's or typed doc's content). Given alone, it reads one level down. The topic list names each doc below a namespace by its identity whatever the detail.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Project directory whose configured integrations contribute topics. Defaults to process.cwd(); an unreadable config falls back to the CLI's own topics.

returns.description: Every reference-doc topic in read order, as DocsListEntry[] ({topic, description, package, replaces?, replacedPackage?}), each readable with docs(topic). meta.namespaces lists the docs tree's top-level namespaces ({topic, description, package}); with depth, each also carries children, the docs below it as a namespace read names them ({topic, description, route, name, package, kind, title, summary, replaces?, replacedPackage?, stability?}), nested the same way to the depth asked for, and childCount where the depth stops on a doc with docs below it. meta.notLoaded names each package whose docs did not load ({package, message}).
One topic's full ReferenceDoc, with token-ref and reference blocks inlined, plus links.
One topic's section index (index: true): {name, title, description, sections: [{id, title, summary}], links}.

One ReferenceSection of the topic, found by key or title, with token-ref and reference blocks inlined. Asked of a docs-tree namespace, it is the section read of the one guide below the namespace that has the section.

A namespace or typed doc in the docs tree, read by its route: {id, route, kind, package, title, summary, breadcrumb, slots, content}. A namespace lists each slot's children one level down, or as deep as depth asks, each child carrying its own slots, childCount where the read stops, and its text at compact or full detail; a typed doc carries its content.

throws.when: depth is not a whole number of levels or 'all'
detail is not brief, compact, or full

the topic is not a string, or matches no topic, no docs-tree route, and no one node of the docs tree by its own name or by its route without the prefix its name repeats; a name more than one node answers to opens none of them, and the suggestions list them

a section is requested but is empty, matches no section, or matches more than one; asked of a docs-tree namespace, when no guide below it or more than one has the section (suggestions name those guides); or asked of a typed doc, which has no sections

examples.label: Every doc below a namespace, one entry each
A namespace and everything below it, in full
A whole guide from the docs tree

doc.name: doctor
doc.summary: Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.
doc.description: Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `{@command init --user}` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli@latest --global}`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:who-answers}.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to diagnose. A directory outside any project, a missing one included, gets the computer checks.

params.name: options.built
params.description: A finished build to check before you deliver it: a project folder, a build output folder, or one built `.html` file, relative to `cwd`. Adds two checks after the others. `built-astryx-usage` fails when the path holds no value import from an Astryx package (any `@astryxdesign/*` package or an integration the project installs), no component imported from one, and no Astryx styles in built CSS or HTML. `built-astryx-purity` warns with the source check of `astryx docs is-my-code-good`: raw elements Astryx has a component for, raw SVG and icon-library icons, inline styles, classes, `stylex.create` and imported stylesheets, each with its file and line, in `.tsx` and `.jsx` files and JSX in `.js` source, found by parsing it; it is info, not inspected, when the path holds no source with JSX, such as a bundle. It reads at most 20,000 files, each up to 5 MB, skipping installs and version control; when either limit leaves source unread and nothing was found, the purity check is info, not fully inspected, and when the file limit ends the read before any Astryx turns up, `built-astryx-usage` warns that the rest went unread instead of failing. Given one built `.html` file, it also reads the local stylesheets and scripts that page links, finding a root-relative link from the nearest folder above the page that holds it; a linked file that is not there makes `built-astryx-usage` warn instead of fail. An empty folder fails with nothing checked, like a missing path. A source tree counts as using Astryx through an import, a re-export (`export … from`) or a stylesheet `@import` of an Astryx package; a type-only import or re-export (`import type`, `export type`, or a list whose names are all `type`) does not count, since the build erases it. `--built` goes with `doctor` alone; a `doctor integration` check refuses it. A path that does not exist fails `built-astryx-usage` with nothing checked, and the purity check is left out. The integrations that count are the dependencies the nearest package.json above the path declares whose installed copy, found the way the CLI autolinks (a hoisted workspace copy included), has an integration manifest. The files under the path, and that configuration, are only read, never run. Without it, doctor runs exactly as before.

returns.description: The diagnostic report: `data.checks`, each with a stable id, label, `status` (`pass` | `warn` | `fail` | `info`), a one-line message, and an optional `fix` (always present on `warn` and `fail`; some `info` checks carry one too); plus `data.summary` with counts per status.

examples.label: Fail a CI step on any failed check
examples.code:
const r = await doctor();
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) process.exitCode = 1;

examples.label: Check a finished build before delivering it
examples.code:
const r = await doctor({built: 'dist'});
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) throw new Error('Not built with Astryx');

doc.name: gapReport
doc.summary: Report a missing or hard-to-use design-system capability to the package that owns it.
doc.description: Routes the report to the package that owns the gap: options.package when given, else the integration whose component replaces the named Core component, else the one package that provides the component, else Core. Sends a gap report to every configured handler: the project config handler first, then each integration handler in config order. Each handler has 30 s to finish, and its output goes to stderr. Public handlers run only with confirmPublic; internal handlers always run. With no handler, it files a GitHub issue for the owning package only with confirmPublic (without it nothing is sent), or returns the package's issues URL when that is not on GitHub. With options.to, the report goes only to that integration's issues URL instead, under the same confirmPublic rule. When loaded integrations name their own issues URLs, the response lists every destination with a line telling an agent to ask the person where to file; pass their choice as options.to, never a package the agent picked itself. The report records whether an agent or a person ran it, and the response lists each handler outcome in order.
doc.signature: gapReport(component: string | undefined, options?: GapReportOptions): Promise<GapReportCategoriesResponse | GapReportReceiptResponse>

params.name: component
params.description: Component or general design-system area, up to 120 characters. Required unless listCategories is true.

params.name: options.category
params.description: Fixed category from the reported category vocabulary. Required unless listCategories is true.

params.name: options.reason
params.description: What capability was missing or difficult, up to 2000 characters. Required unless listCategories is true.

params.name: options.detail
params.description: Optional additional context (up to 8000 characters).

params.name: options.package
params.description: Package that owns the gap: @astryxdesign/core, or a loaded integration by package name or config entry. Overrides automatic owner routing, which picks the integration whose component replaces the named Core component, else the one package that provides it, else Core; required when more than one package provides the component.

params.name: options.confirmPublic
params.description: Allow public delivery: public handlers run, and a GitHub issues URL gets an issue filed through the gh CLI.

params.name: options.to
params.description: A destination the person chose: a loaded integration whose manifest names an issues URL. The report goes only to that issues URL; handlers do not run.

params.name: options.listCategories
params.description: Return categories, and the destinations in meta when there is more than one, without resolving a route or writing; the component and every other option are refused with ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory used to load project config and component ownership.

returns.description: The fixed category values and labels.

Receipt: status (filed, partial, failed, routed_only, consent_required, skipped), package, issuesUrl, ordered deliveries (handlerType, handler, audience, status, url, message), filedCount, and routedOnlyCount.

throws.when: component, category, or reason is missing, blank, or not a string (unless listCategories is true)
category is not one of the fixed gap-report values
component is over 120 characters, category is over 80, reason is over 2000, or detail is not a string or is over 8000 characters
more than one package owns the named component
the explicitly selected package is not loaded, or options.to names no destination (the error lists the destinations)
no report handler is configured and the owning package has no issues URL

examples.label: Route without public mutation
examples.code: const receipt = await gapReport('Button', {category: 'missing_variant', reason: 'Need a compact size'});

examples.label: Name the owning package
examples.code: const receipt = await gapReport('Button', {category: 'docs_gap', reason: 'Missing keyboard example', package: '@astryxdesign/core'});

doc.name: hook
doc.summary: Resolve a hook by name, or list the catalog, with an optional params-only slice.
doc.description: Routes on its arguments: a name returns that hook's full authored HookDoc; no name (or `list`/`category`) returns the catalog grouped by category. The `params` flag narrows a single hook to just its parameters table.
doc.signature: hook(name?: string, options?: HookOptions): Promise<HookListResponse | HookDetailResponse | HookDetailParamsResponse>

params.name: name
params.description: Hook name to resolve (e.g. 'useMediaQuery'). Omit to list the catalog.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to resolve @astryxdesign/core from.

params.name: options.list
params.description: Return the grouped catalog instead of a single hook.

params.name: options.category
params.description: List only the hooks in this category, a key of the unfiltered list such as 'Media' or 'Focus'.

params.name: options.params
params.description: Return only the hook's parameters table.

params.name: options.detail
params.description: Detail level for list views.
params.default: 'full' for a named hook; 'brief' for lists (returned as data.detail: 'names')

params.name: options.lang
params.description: Language code for localized doc content.

doc.summary: Add an icon set to an integration package.
doc.description: Creates an integration manifest when the package has none, writes the set directory with its strongly typed same-stem IconSetDoc and a starter data file (schemaVersion 1, module set to the package name, no icons and an empty map yet), and the set's generated module with its declaration file and an empty themeIcons theme map; with from, it wraps a library's icons into them, records the installed library and version as the data file's source, copies the library's license notices into the set, uses the library's license, maps each Astryx definition whose name is an icon id, and returns up to three likely icons for each other definition as suggestions (by its name, its words, and the other names the library gives an icon; never a part of a word, a negated form, or the opposite direction), never written. A library whose export names end in style, size and weight words gives one icon per glyph, named without those words, in the look the default variant names, else the library's usual default (outline, regular, the middle weight). Over an existing set, `from` refreshes it; without `from`, `variants`, `defaultVariant`, `displayName` and `description` update it in place and leave its icons, map and generated module unchanged (a variant an icon has must stay declared, and a set with icons keeps its default variant). It declares the manifest's `experimental.iconSets` root on first use, and includes the manifest and root in package.json files when the package already uses an allowlist. It never writes the package's entry, exports, main, types, files list, peers, or scripts: its notes name each change the package needs as text to copy. Every path is confined to the package, and an existing set is changed only as above. Experimental: it may change or be removed in a patch release.

doc.name: init
doc.summary: Non-interactive project setup: install agent docs and point at the theme + build workflows.
doc.description: Sets a project up with NO prompts, so it behaves identically for humans, agents, CI, and piped I/O. By default it writes the agent-docs cheat sheet, including guidance from configured integrations, at the project root (the nearest package.json that declares an @astryxdesign package, else the nearest package.json, searching no higher than the repository root): to AGENTS.md, to the project's Claude Code file (CLAUDE.md, else .claude/CLAUDE.md; when CLAUDE.md exists, a block in .claude/CLAUDE.md is removed, unless the project ignores CLAUDE.md, in which case a .claude/CLAUDE.md the project commits keeps a copy), and as a one-line import of AGENTS.md in GEMINI.md unless GEMINI.md already imports it. In the home folder, or in a settings folder in it outside a project, it writes none: every folder of the home folder whose name starts with a dot is a settings folder, and such a folder itself never counts as a project, even with a package.json; a folder below it with a package.json does. The managed block is Astryx-owned: it is written, refreshed, and removed whatever ignore rules or generated markers say, and the text around it is never changed. It then prints getting-started guidance; `features` / `all` print only the chosen features' guidance instead (the theme feature also writes the annotated theme template). With `removeAgents` it removes the managed agent-docs block, at the project root and in `ctx.cwd`, instead of installing. Outside a project it writes the same files but prints no getting-started steps and no step that adds a theme to an app, since those set up a project the folder does not have. With `user` it sets up the computer instead of the folder: it writes the computer-level agent text, one skill file at `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, linked into the skill folders of agents that read only their own (`~/.claude/skills` always; Kiro, Windsurf, Letta, Xcode's coding assistant, and `~/.config/agents/skills` when that folder exists), with a managed copy for Continue, whose scanner skips links,, telling agents anywhere on the computer that Astryx is there and when to use it; with `user` and `removeAgents` it removes the file and the links it made and records that the text is turned off. The CLI installed for the computer refreshes the file in the background after each upgrade; package install scripts, project setup, and upgrade never write it. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it writes the agent docs and prints no getting-started steps; `user` writes only the agent guide for the computer, in the home folder, and touches nothing in `cwd`. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.

params.name: options.user

The text uses the `astryx` command, or the command of the host that started the run; an integration's `cliCommand` never applies. Records the links it made, or with `removeAgents` that the text is turned off, in `astryx/settings.json` in the per-user configuration folder. A file without the Astryx markers, one edited since Astryx wrote it, or a symlink, is kept as it is, and so is anything at a link target that Astryx did not create. When no `astryx` command on the computer runs the Astryx CLI, the text is still written and the receipt carries a warning to install the CLI for the computer (`npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli`). doc.name: integrationCheck
doc.summary: Run every source check against the integration package in the current folder, as its build does: validate, components, templates, and docs.
doc.description: Runs `validateIntegration`, `integrationComponentConflicts`, `integrationTemplateConflicts`, and `integrationDocConflicts` against the integration package in `options.cwd`, and counts each result the way that check's own subcommand exits. The run fails when any of the four would fail on its own. With `strict` it also fails on any warning and on any check that did not run: a package with no integration manifest, or a comparison a check carries that was skipped, such as one that needs the project's TypeScript. `strict` adds no check: it reports those warnings and skipped work again, as errors in the checks' own issue format. A new check, or a new failure code, joins only in a minor release, named in the release notes.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: The integration package folder to check.

params.name: options.strict
params.description: Also fail on any warning and on any check that did not run, not only on errors. A malformed `cliCommand` is reported as a note (`invalid_cli_command`) in `data.notes` of the validate check, which fails nothing until a minor release names it.

params.name: options.next
params.description: Also count the findings the next minor release turns into warnings, validate's notes marked `next`, as warnings now, so `strict` fails on them.

returns.description: `data.validated` (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was checked), `data.name` and `data.version` of the package, `data.strict`, `data.next`, and `data.checks`, one entry per check in the order they run (`validate`, `components`, `templates`, `docs`), each with `check`, `errors` (what makes that check's own subcommand exit 1), `warnings`, `skipped` (why work did not run), `failed` (whether that subcommand exits 1), and `response`, the envelope the check returns on its own. The totals are `data.errors`, `data.warnings`, and `data.skipped` (each reason prefixed with its check); an issue every check starts from, such as one about the manifest, counts once, and every other finding counts on its own. `data.unchecked` counts the items the checks list as not compared, which never fail it. `data.upcoming` counts the findings the next minor release turns into warnings (validate's notes marked `next`), and `data.next` says whether this run counted them as warnings now. With `strict`, `data.failures` lists each warning and each piece of skipped work once again as an error in the checks' own issue format ({check, severity: `error`, code, message, component, prop, fix, file, line}, each where it applies); it is empty without `strict`. `data.failed` decides the exit code.

examples.label: Fail on warnings too
examples.code:
const {data} = await integrationCheck({strict: true});
if (data.failed) process.exitCode = 1;

doc.name: integrationComponentConflicts
doc.summary: Check integration component names, replaces declarations, and documented props.
doc.description: Loads one local or installed integration, compares its component names with Core, and returns non-blocking conflicts with the exact package-qualified component command required to keep an intentional overlap. Each component's replaces is checked too: its findings are issues, errors for a package that declares the CLI range that turns replacement on and warnings otherwise. A `{@link}` in a component doc's text that names no doc is an `invalid_doc_graph` warning, since it prints as written. Each component doc's props are compared with the component's TypeScript props, read with the project's own `typescript` (or, where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, the `@typescript/typescript6` it installs): a documented prop the code lacks, a prop the package declares that the doc omits, a wrong `required`, or a type that does not match. A type is judged only when it reads exactly: the same text as the source, once whitespace, quotes and union order are set aside (exactly, if it contains `readonly`), or primitives, literals, arrays and unions of those, or a name for one, on both sides, a field such as `status.type` included, and for a union of props types, the type of any one member. A field the prop's variants give different types is listed when the doc gives only some variants' types. A mutable array type matches a readonly one, because callers can pass it; a readonly one documented for a mutable array is a mismatch. `Name = …` with a union after it must match in both parts; one value after it (`Size = 'md'`) is read as a default. A name only TypeScript's own libraries declare is not resolved, and `React.X` resolves through React where the prop is declared. Every other type is listed as not compared, never reported, and so is a name an index signature takes unless exactly one the package declares takes it; with a TypeScript older than 4.8 no type is judged. Those findings are warnings in `propDrift`; without TypeScript it is `skipped` with a reason.

params.name: pkg
params.description: Installed package; omit for the local package.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Resolution directory.

returns.description: `validated` (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was inspected), integration identity, structural and replaces issues, and Core component-name conflicts with package-qualified commands. An active replacement that keeps the Core name it replaces is not a conflict. When the manifest loads and declares a components root, `propDrift` holds the props comparison: `status` (`checked` | `skipped`), `reason` when skipped, `typescript`, `components` compared, `typesCompared` (documented prop types judged), `typesSkipped` (why none was, with a TypeScript older than 4.8), `findings` ({component, prop, kind: `not_in_code` | `not_in_doc` | `required_mismatch` | `type_mismatch` | `default_mismatch`, severity: `warning`, message, doc, source, docType?, codeType?, docRequired?, codeRequired?, docDefault?, codeDefault?, fix?}), `unchecked` ({component, doc, reason}), `typesNotCompared` ({component, doc, reason, props}: every other documented prop type, grouped by why it was not judged: not a form the check judges exactly (a doc type that does not parse, or a prop a mapped type builds from keys the check cannot trace, included), a field the prop's variants give different types, a standard prop such as `className`, or a prop declared outside the package), and `propsNotChecked` when a mapped type builds props from keys the check cannot trace to the package ({component, doc, reason, props}: no warning is drawn for those props).

doc.name: integrationDocConflicts
doc.summary: Check an integration's docs: the docs tree they add, every link, and overlaps with Core topics.
doc.description: Loads one local or installed integration and classifies Core doc overlaps as intentional replacements, intentional extensions, or accidental same-name conflicts that need an explicit relationship or a rename. `copiedPassages` lists each pair of topics that repeat 10 or more words of prose word for word: two of the package's topics, or one of them and a Core topic other than the one it replaces. Code and examples are not compared. `fluff` lists each padding phrase, with its file line, and each topic of 80 or more prose words in which fewer than half carry content. `strayPointers` lists each code span that is exactly `{@command docs <name>}` for a doc that exists, in a topic's prose, description or summary or a component doc's text fields, with the `{@link}` that replaces it. Each entry of these lists is also a warning (`copied_passage`, `doc_fluff`, `stray_doc_pointer`), so `integration check --strict` fails on it; the check itself still fails only on errors.

params.name: pkg
params.description: Installed package; omit for the local package.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Resolution directory.

returns.description: `validated` (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was inspected), integration identity, structural issues, classified Core doc relationships, `copiedPassages`, `fluff`, and `strayPointers`.

doc.name: integrationPackCheck
doc.summary: Check an integration package the way npm will publish it.
doc.description: Validates the local integration, runs the package lifecycle, packs with npm, checks required files against npm's authoritative tarball list, extracts the real tarball into a scratch consumer, compares local and packed contribution inventories, and resolves every packed component through its documented public import to verify that module exports the component. A package that ships a namespace doc or a placed guide, or has a template that sets `replaces`, fails unless its `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range admits only CLIs that read them.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory inside the integration package.

returns.description: Package identity, tarball facts, local and packed inventories, and issues.

doc.name: integrationTemplateConflicts
doc.summary: Find integration template ids that also exist in Core.
doc.description: Loads one local or installed integration, compares its template ids with the built-in Core page and block templates, and returns non-blocking conflicts with the exact package-qualified CLI command required to keep an intentional overlap.

params.name: pkg
params.description: Installed integration package; omit to inspect the local package.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory used to resolve the local or installed integration.

returns.description: `validated` (false when no integration manifest was found, so nothing was inspected and the empty conflict list carries no information), the integration identity, structural issues, and every Core template-id conflict with a package-qualified command.

doc.name: summarizeIssues
doc.summary: Tally integration issues by severity into error and warning counts.
doc.description: A synchronous helper that reduces an AstryxIntegrationIssue[] (as returned by validateIntegration) to counts of errors and warnings: the seam a caller uses to decide an exit code or print a summary line. Issues of any other severity are ignored.

params.name: issues
params.description: The issues to tally (e.g. `data.issues` from validateIntegration).

returns.name: errors
returns.description: Count of issues with severity "error".

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: Count of issues with severity "warning".

doc.name: validateIntegration
doc.summary: Validate a single Astryx integration package and report its issues.
doc.description: Validates exactly ONE integration at a time: the local package rooted at cwd (no `pkg`), or an installed package resolved from cwd/node_modules (`pkg` given). It loads and schema-checks the manifest, verifies each declared contribution root exists, and runs the codemod/template/component/docs/theme validators, returning every finding as an AstryxIntegrationIssue. A missing local manifest is guidance (name null, no issues), not an error, so callers can stay exit-0 in a non-integration directory. It also checks every doc the package ships under its roots (component, template, docs topic, theme, and translation, served or not) against the published authoring type for its kind, as `tsc` would, with the project's own `typescript` (or, where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, the `@typescript/typescript6` it installs): an unknown field, a missing required field, or a value outside a field's type is a warning in `docTypes` naming the field and a fix. A test fixture under `__tests__` in the components or docs root is counted, not checked. Without TypeScript, `docTypes` is `skipped` with a reason.

params.name: pkg
params.description: Installed package name to validate; omit to validate the package rooted at cwd.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to resolve the local package / node_modules from.

returns.description: The result envelope: `data.validated`, false when nothing was validated — with no `package.json` at all, `data.issues` carries one `no_package` error-severity issue so the command exits 1; with a `package.json` but no integration manifest, `data.issues` is empty, which means "not looked at", not "healthy"; `data.name` and `data.version` of the validated package (both null when `data.validated` is false; `data.name` is `(local package)` when the local package.json has no readable name), plus `data.issues`, an AstryxIntegrationIssue[] of {code, severity: `warning` | `error`, message, fix?, file?, line?}: `fix` is the change that resolves the issue, and `file` and `line` where it is, relative to the package, when the check knows them; and `data.notes` when there are any: {code, message, next?} information beside the issues; a note fails nothing by default, and one with `next: true` counts as a warning under `integration check --next`, fails `integration check --strict --next`, and fails `--strict` from the next minor release. Notes include `invalid_cli_command` for a `cliCommand` that was ignored as malformed and `cli_peer_version` when the running CLI is outside the `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range of the package, and the package layout findings added after the last minor release, each with its fix in the message: `duplicate_component_doc`, `symlinked_root`, `unreadable_file`, `invalid_package_json` (no `name` or `version`), `no_provider_id`, and `source_without_component_doc` for a doc whose file name differs from its source only in letter case where the two still pair; and `doc_name_mismatch` and `unknown_block_component` (see `docNames` and `blockComponents`); they become warnings in the next minor release. For the commands a topic writes, `runner_command` (written with a package runner), `plain_command` (written bare), `package_manager_command` (written for one package manager) and `doc_token` (a token that does not parse) notes each give the file, line and the token to write. A `doc_target_not_found` note names a doc whose `replaces` or `extends` names no topic and no guide of the CLI's docs or the package's own (such as a namespace, with the guides below it), so it changes nothing unless an app also installs a package that provides it, and a `doc_section_unplaced` note a section whose `before` or `after` names no section of the topic or guide it extends, so it is added at the end, and a `duplicate_guide_replacement` note two docs of the package that replace one guide, of which only the last is read; they become warnings in the next minor release. When the manifest loads, `data.docTypes` holds the doc type check: `status` (`checked` | `skipped`), `reason` when skipped, `typescript`, `docs` (doc values checked), `findings` ({doc, line, export, type, field, problem: `unknown_field` | `missing_field` | `wrong_type`, severity: `warning`, message, fix}), `unchecked` ({doc, reason}: a doc that could not be fully checked, or a root its reader cannot read), and `fixtures` when the components or docs root holds test fixture docs under `__tests__`: how many, none of them checked. When the manifest loads, `data.docNames` lists the component doc names it could not judge: `status` (`checked`), `findings` (always empty; a doc name the module its import names provably does not export is a `doc_name_mismatch` note, with its fix in the message) and `unchecked` ({file, name, reason}: a doc whose `name` differs from the name it is listed under and whose source exports cannot all be read, such as a re-export from another package). When the manifest loads, `data.blockComponents` lists the component names templates give in `exampleFor` or `componentsUsed` that could not be judged: `status` (`checked`), `findings` (always empty; a name neither the package nor Core has, and the template does not import, is an `unknown_block_component` note, with its fix in the message) and `unchecked` ({file, name, reason}: a name the template may reach through anything other than named imports and re-exports from Core, React, StyleX, local helpers or the entry of the package itself, such as an import from another package, a default or namespace import, an alias of or member read off an imported binding, require() or a dynamic import(), or a local module that cannot be read, or any name Core would have to resolve when Core is not installed). Since 0.7.3 each import apps cannot use is a note in `data.notes`, its fix inside the message, listed only: it does not fail this command or `integration check --strict`, and fails `--strict` from the next minor release. The codes are `component_import_not_exported`, `component_import_other_package`, `component_import_missing_name`, `example_import_not_exported`, `example_import_missing_name`, `template_import_not_exported`, `template_import_outside_root`, `template_private_import`, `template_import_missing_name` and `template_no_default_export`. Since 0.7.4 the examples a package ships are checked the same way: `component_without_example` (a published component no block template shows with `exampleFor` and `isShowcase: true`, or names in `alsoShowcaseFor`), `template_category` (a template category written as a path, such as `components/X`), `showcase_not_standalone` (a showcase that imports server-only code or reads `process.env` past `NODE_ENV`) and `template_asset_not_packed` (a `new URL(…, import.meta.url)` asset that is missing, or that `npm pack --dry-run` leaves out of the package). When npm cannot list the package's files, an asset no `files` entry can reach is still a note, and any other is listed in `data.exampleAssets` (`{status: 'checked', findings: [], unchecked}`, present only when it lists any) as {file, asset, reason}; `integration check` counts them as not compared. When the manifest loads, `data.publicImports` is `{status: 'checked', findings: [], unchecked}`: `unchecked` lists each import the check could not judge, as {file, specifier, reason}, the reason starting `example <label>:` for an import in a component example: an `exports` target not built yet; a module whose export list cannot be read in full (CommonJS, or a declaration file it cannot read); a root import in a package with no `exports` (the root module `main` names is not read); every name an import (other than a component doc's own component) names that its module does not export, while a TypeScript file in the package has a `declare module` block for a relative path or the package's own name or a subpath of it, which can add names to that module (a `declare module` in a comment, `declare global`, a wildcard such as `'*.css'`, and another package's name do not count; a file whose text has `declare module` but that cannot be parsed counts); the same for every such name when the package has more than 5,000 files to search for that block; a deep path into build output not built yet in a package with no `exports`; a template import of Core when `@astryxdesign/core` is not installed beside the package (a `packages/core` of the workspace under another name does not count); every import of the package's own name when package.json has no `name` or a `name` that is not a bare package name; one entry for the whole check when package.json cannot be read; and an import of a subpath whose `exports` entry has only a `types` target, unless it is `import type`, every binding is an inline `type`, or every name it imports is a type its types file declares: a value import of a name that file does not declare as a type, a namespace or side-effect import, or any import when the types file cannot be read (it may be build output). `integration check` counts the unchecked as not compared; they never fail it. `data.olderCliNotes` ({file, kind: `template` | `namespace`, field, message}), for the local package, lists each descriptor field a release before 0.7.4 refuses while the package's CLI peer range admits one, such as `stability` on a template or namespace doc; it is present only when it has entries, is never counted, and never fails a check.

doc.name: assertResponse
doc.summary: Parse and assert one expected response type, throwing on an error or a mismatch.
doc.description: The strict alternative to parseResponse + manual narrowing: it parses, rethrows a CLIError as an Error carrying the CLI message, and rejects any envelope whose `type` is not the one you asked for. Use it when a call site expects exactly one response type and any other outcome is a bug worth failing on.

params.name: raw
params.description: The CLI stdout to parse: a JSON string, or an object that was already parsed.

params.name: expectedType
params.description: The response discriminant the caller requires (e.g. 'component.detail').

returns.description: The parsed envelope, guaranteed at runtime to carry the requested `type`. The published signature is untyped; cast to the matching *Response type for typed access.

throws.when: a plain Error with no code: the CLI returned an error envelope (its message is rethrown; code and suggestions are dropped), or the response `type` is not expectedType

examples.label: Require one type
examples.code:
const r = assertResponse(stdout, 'component.detail');
r.data.name; // safe: any other outcome threw

doc.name: isError
doc.summary: Did the CLI return an error envelope?
doc.description: Tests a parsed response for an `error` key. Branch on this before touching `data`, and prefer the stable `code` field over matching the human-readable message, which is not a contract. Note this returns a plain boolean, not a TypeScript type predicate, so it does not narrow on its own: cast to the matching *Response type to get typed access.

params.name: result
params.description: A parsed response envelope, typically from parseResponse().

returns.description: True when the value is a non-null object carrying an `error` key (a CLIError envelope).

examples.label: Branch on the stable code

doc.name: parseResponse
doc.summary: Parse `astryx --json` stdout into the structural response envelope.
doc.description: The entry point for consuming the CLI as a subprocess. A JSON string is parsed; an already-parsed object is passed through unchanged, so it is safe to call on either. It returns the structural { apiVersion, type, data, meta? } envelope without narrowing: `data` stays unknown until you discriminate on `type` (or use assertResponse).

params.name: raw
params.description: The CLI stdout to parse: a JSON string, or an object that was already parsed.

returns.description: The { apiVersion, type, data, meta? } envelope, or a CLIError envelope ({ apiVersion, error, code, suggestions? }). The published signature is intentionally untyped; narrow it by casting to the matching *Response type exported from @astryxdesign/cli/json.

throws.when: raw is a string that is not valid JSON (surfaced from JSON.parse)

examples.label: Parse then narrow
examples.code:
const result = parseResponse(stdout);
if (isError(result)) throw new Error(result.error);

doc.name: render
doc.summary: Render a page to one self-contained HTML file, or turn a rendered file back into a page.
doc.description: Renders the page module's default export on the server with the project's own React and Astryx components (outside a project, with the Astryx, React and StyleX the CLI runs with), and writes ONE static HTML file that needs nothing beside it: the page's own StyleX styles are compiled, Core's stylesheets are cut to the rules the markup uses (layer order, custom properties and keyframes kept), local images become data: URIs, and the page's source is embedded so it can be given back exactly. The file runs no script and loads nothing from the network, so it works inside a sandboxed frame with a strict content security policy, and its colors follow the viewer's light or dark scheme. Warnings name anything that may differ from what the author meant, such as a component that did not render the text it was given. With `reverse`, it writes the embedded source back byte for byte, and only the files a render embeds: the page and the local modules, stylesheets, JSON files and images it imports, into a new folder; a file with Astryx markup but no embedded source is rebuilt from its component class names and data attributes (text and layout only); any other file is refused. Experimental: it may change or be removed in a patch release.
doc.signature: render(file: string, options?: RenderOptions): Promise<RenderPageResponse | RenderReverseResponse>

params.name: file
params.description: The page module (.tsx, .jsx, .ts, .js or .mjs) with a default export, or with `reverse` the rendered .html file.

params.name: options.out
params.description: The file to write. Rendering: an .html file (default: the page's name with .html). Reversing: a page module (default: inside a new folder beside the HTML file, named after it, such as `report-restored/`).

params.name: options.reverse
params.description: Turn a rendered HTML file back into a page module.

params.name: options.title
params.description: The rendered page's title (default: its first top-level heading, else the file name). Rendering only.

params.name: options.overwrite
params.description: Replace the existing page module when reversing (never a protected file, and never a file other than the page, which always goes into a new folder). Rendering replaces an existing HTML file only when a render wrote it.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Folder relative paths resolve from (default: the current directory).

returns.description: The page and the HTML file written, its size, the local modules embedded, the stylesheets inlined, the class and image counts, the CSS size, and any warnings.
How the page came back (`embedded`, exact; or `rebuilt`, text and layout only), the files written, and for a rebuilt page the components it uses and what could not be rebuilt.

throws.when: no file is given

the file or `out` has the wrong kind of extension, `out` is the input itself, `title` is given with `reverse`, or `overwrite` without it; with `reverse`, the page would land under a configuration name (`vite.config.ts`) or where a test, story or benchmark runner would run it (judged from the repository root)
the file, or a local file the page imports, does not exist

rendering would replace an existing file a render did not write, reversing would replace an existing file and `overwrite` is not set, or an existing file the project protects (generated, vendored or ignored) would be replaced, which `overwrite` never does
a file cannot be written, such as when `out` names a folder; with `reverse`, every file is written or none is
the page does not compile, or a stylesheet it imports is not valid CSS (the message names the file)
the page has no default export
the page imports a package that is not installed; the suggestion is its install line
outside a project, the page imports an Astryx package, React or StyleX, and the Core of the release that answers cannot be downloaded
the page reads a browser-only API, such as window or document, while rendering
a local file the page uses is over 8 MB
the page does not finish rendering within 60 seconds
the page throws while rendering for any other reason
reversing a file a render did not write, with no embedded source and no Astryx markup; the suggestion is `astryx build "<what the page is>"`

reversing a file a render wrote whose embedded source was removed (and that has no Astryx components to rebuild from), a file whose embedded source is damaged, lists a path twice, carries a module, stylesheet or JSON file the page does not reach through its imports, or an image, font or media file whose bytes are not one, or carries a file a render never embeds (a dotfile or dot-folder, `node_modules`, a package manifest, lockfile or tool configuration, or any kind but a page module, stylesheet, JSON or image)

a file would be written outside the current folder (symlinks followed), or through a symbolic link: `out`, or with `reverse` the page or an embedded file; or, with `reverse`, a file other than the page would go into a folder that already exists

doc.name: exportSearchIndex
doc.summary: The candidates search ranks in a folder, as plain JSON to store and rank later with rankSearchIndex().
doc.description: Gathers what `search()` would rank in `cwd` and returns it as `{version, candidates}`. Gathering reads each installed package's docs and loads its integration manifest, which runs that package's code, so a catalog that lists packages it must not load makes the index where loading is safe (a folder with those packages installed), stores it, and ranks it with {@link function:rankSearchIndex}. With `package`, the index keeps only that package's candidates, for a catalog that stores one index per package. A component description's inline doc tokens are resolved where the index is made, as `search` prints them; when Core could not be had there, the index says why in `coreSkipped`. Fields that point into the folder are left out, so an index reads the same wherever it was made. The candidates are the ranker's input, not a stable shape: an index is ranked only by the CLI version that made it. Experimental: it may change or be removed in a patch release.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: The folder to gather from, read as `search()` reads it.

params.name: options.package
params.description: Keep only the candidates this npm package owns: its components, templates, themes, and doc parts. Without it the index holds everything the folder's search ranks, Core's entries and the CLI's docs included.

returns.description: `version`, the CLI version that made it, and `candidates`, the gathered entries as plain JSON.

throws.when: `package` is given and is not a non-empty string

doc.name: rankSearchIndex
doc.summary: Ranks stored search indexes with search's own tree: an index made in one folder answers as search() does there.
doc.description: Ranks the candidates of every index together, with the same tree, weights, and order as {@link function:search}. An index made with `exportSearchIndex()` in one folder ranks exactly as `search(query)` does in that folder: the same results, order, and scores. Indexes made in separate folders are ranked together as one list; a doc that one package replaces or extends in another is not merged across them, so a project's own `search` can differ where that happens. A theme result's command is the in-project `theme add`. When every index was made where Core could not be had, an open rank (no `type`) carries `meta.partial`, as `search` does; a rank of `type` `component`, `hook`, or `template` throws the error `search` throws there. Every index must come from this CLI's version, because the candidates' shape is the ranker's input. Experimental: it may change or be removed in a patch release.

doc.name: search
doc.summary: Unified ranked search across components, hooks, docs, templates, and themes.
doc.description: The single "I'm looking for X" entry point across every content domain. Matching and scores are keyword + fuzzy (not embeddings). Between score bands results keep the lexical order, whose domain priority can put a weaker component, hook, template, or theme above a stronger doc, and a query that is an entry's exact name answers with that entry first. Inside a band, fixed weights order the matches, so a description match can lead a keyword match in the same band (55–99 holds both). A component's usage guidance (its best practices) is indexed one tier below its description, so the words a reader types still find it. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, items from integrations installed next to this CLI package globally are searched too, and theme results name no step that adds a theme to an app; inside a project, only the project's own integrations count. See {@link namespace:global} and {@link generic:computer-integrations}.

params.name: query
params.description: Free-text search term.

params.name: options.type
params.description: Restrict results to a single domain.

params.name: options.limit
params.description: Maximum number of results.

params.name: options.cwd
params.description: Directory to resolve @astryxdesign/core from: the project's installed Core, else, outside a project or in a project with nothing installed, the Core of the release that answers, installed into the per-user cache first when needed. A docs-only or themes-only search (`type: 'doc'` or `type: 'theme'`) does not need it. A search with no `type` covers the docs and themes alone only when that Core cannot be obtained, and then says so in `meta.partial`.

returns.description: The query echoed back, `matchCount` (how many candidates matched in total, before `limit`), plus a ranked SearchResultEntry[] bounded by `limit`: each has domain, name, score, reason, description, and follow-up command, plus `import` for components and hooks, `title` for docs, `displayName` and `kind` for templates, and `displayName` for themes. A deprecated component's result also carries `deprecated`, `{replacement, description}` from its doc: the name of the component to use instead and the modernization route. A doc result is the smallest part that answers: one section (with `section`, and a command that reads only it), one docs-tree route, or a topic, whose command lists its sections. `parent` is the command that opens the level above it: the section list of its topic, the namespace a tree node sits in, the topic level (Guides or Foundations) for a flat topic, or the topic list for a top-level namespace. Every doc result also carries `package`, the npm package that authored it (for a section, the package its file came from). A theme result is one theme you can import: `name` is its slug, its command is `{@command theme add <slug>}` (outside a project, where there is no app to add it to, `{@command theme eject <slug>}`), and `package` is the npm package that ships it (`@astryxdesign/cli` for the CLI's own themes). When a search with no `type` could not obtain @astryxdesign/core, `meta.partial` is `{skipped, reason}`: the domains it skipped (`component`, `hook`, `template`) and why; the results are the docs and themes, and text mode prints one line on standard error.

@astryxdesign/core cannot be found from the cwd, and `type` names a domain that reads it: `component`, `hook`, or `template`

doc.name: swizzle
doc.summary: Eject a component's source into your project for customization.
doc.description: Ejects a component's source into the consumer project for deep customization. It copies from the locally resolved @astryxdesign/core (or the owning integration) package source. Every import in the copy names a file the copy holds or a path the owner package exports: names the package exports are imported from its public paths, and every internal module the component needs is copied beside it in the package's folder layout. Tests, stories and docs are not copied. An output folder swizzle owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before) gets an astryx-swizzle.json marker naming each package its copies came from, with its version, so @astryxdesign/build's Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, and withAstryx() under webpack, compile the copy below the theme. The receipt flags whether any copied file uses StyleX and lists each npm package the copy imports with the range the owner package declares. With no name (or list) it returns the swizzlable component names instead. An integration component that replaces a Core component is what that Core name copies; options.package '@astryxdesign/core' copies the original. The list names Core components, including one an integration component replaces.

doc.name: generateTonalPalette
doc.summary: Generate candidate tonal palette data without filesystem effects.
doc.description: Runs the versioned astryx-oklch-v1 authoring recipe. The returned candidate contains exact hex values for review; it does not modify a theme, write files, perform semantic mapping, or make accessibility claims. Stop numbers remain stable across layouts, and requested decimal stops are emitted explicitly. Anchor policies are intentional: exact preserves the chosen color at its stop; bounded permits movement within maxDeltaE; flexible treats it as guidance. An anchor needs a mode and stop. Stops apply to every family in one request. The candidate always exposes standalone black and white values for direct theme authoring. Generated TypeScript exports them as `black` and `white`, so they can be assigned directly to semantic theme tokens. Those names are reserved and cannot be used as tonal family IDs. The default 0–100 layout also repeats them as family endpoints; a custom stop list can omit those repeated endpoints.

params.name: input
params.description: Families and seeds plus optional modes, shared stops, anchors, vibrancy from 0 to 100 (default 50), and neutral profile.

returns.description: Deterministic candidate data for author review, including a stops array that defines ramp iteration order and standalone black and white values outside the tonal families.

throws.when: the request, family, seed, stop layout, mode, or anchor is invalid

examples.label: Preserve a required brand color
examples.code: generateTonalPalette({stops: [50], families: [{id: 'brand', seed: '#0074e2', anchors: [{mode: 'light', stop: 50, color: '#1682d5', policy: 'exact'}]}]});

examples.label: Allow limited anchor movement
examples.code: generateTonalPalette({stops: [50], families: [{id: 'brand', seed: '#0074e2', anchors: [{mode: 'light', stop: 50, color: '#1682d5', policy: 'bounded', maxDeltaE: 2}]}]});

examples.label: Use an anchor as guidance
examples.code: generateTonalPalette({stops: [50], families: [{id: 'pink', seed: '#ff4db8', anchors: [{mode: 'light', stop: 50, color: '#ff4db8', policy: 'flexible'}]}]});
