An integration's namespace doc without a `placement` is a top-level level of the tree, and its guides name it with `placement`; a doc can be placed only in a namespace of its own package. When two packages claim one route, the CLI's own docs win, then integrations in configured order, and `astryx doctor` names the loser.

Child docs request one canonical home with placement. A collection block refers to those docs by stable reference and never creates a second identity or parent. It is not rendered yet: `astryx doctor` warns on one.

items: Use a directory as implicit navigation.
Put JSX, HTML, ANSI, callbacks, or custom renderer code in a doc.
Use choice, callout, or checklist blocks before the full block-extension contract exists.

content.text: The doc-type for a reference/topic doc: tokens, principles, theming, patterns, accessibility, migration guides. Unlike ComponentDoc it is not tied to a component: drop a `.doc.mjs` in the docs directory and it shows up in `astryx docs`. Content is built from ordered sections of mixed content blocks.
Applies to: <topic>.doc.{ts,mjs,js} in the folder the integration manifest's `docs` names

rows: Doc-kind discriminant. Stays 'generic' (the reference/topic discriminant). Legacy `export const docs = {...}` docs omit it.
URL-safe identifier, used as the CLI topic name. e.g. 'tokens', 'principles'.
Human-readable title. e.g. 'All Tokens'. (Reference docs use `title`, not `displayName`.)
One-line summary shown in topic listings.

Words a reader may search for that the title and sections do not use: a synonym, a task, or another library's name for the same thing. `astryx search` matches each as a keyword of the whole topic, so an exact one ranks the topic like its own title does. Example: ['dark mode', 'color scheme'].

Name of an existing topic this doc takes the place of. Authored by an integration that serves its own guide instead of the built-in one: on a doc of the same name it swaps the content, and on a doc of another name it also leaves the old name as an alias so `astryx docs <old>` still resolves. Exclusive with `extends`. Example: 'getting-started'.

Name of an existing topic this doc merges onto, section by section. A section replaces the base section with the same `id`, or else the one with exactly its title when either of the two has no `id`. A key derived from a title counts only against an `id`: a section without an `id` also matches a base section whose `id` is the key its title derives, and a section with an `id` also matches a base section without one whose title derives that `id`. Two different `id`s never match, two sections without an `id` whose titles differ only in case or punctuation stay separate, and a section that matches none is appended. The topic keeps the base's title and description. For correcting or adding to a topic rather than owning it. Exclusive with `replaces`. Example: 'theme'.
Ordered sections that make up the doc. Each becomes an h2 in full output and can be retrieved via `astryx docs <topic> <section>`.

Stable section anchor. New docs should set this instead of relying on a mutable title. Published @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.3 and earlier reject the field and hide every doc topic the package ships, so `astryx integration verify` fails an integration that sets one until it declares an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`.
Navigation category ('guide' | 'foundations'). Mirrors the parent doc's category so sections can be grouped independently.

Ordered content blocks: prose, heading, code, table, list, token-ref, and reference. A `reference` block (`{type: 'reference', target, projection?, presentation?}`) includes another doc from its canonical source instead of a copy: a schema, command, function, or enum doc as `astryx docs` prints it, then the command that opens it. `projection.fields` keeps only those fields of a schema; `presentation` is `full` (the default), `compact` (no code blocks), or `summary` (only the doc's title, summary, and command). Any other doc shows as a summary. Graph-only workflow and collection blocks are available through GraphContentBlock on NamespaceDoc, without widening the stable ReferenceContentBlock union. Inside text, `{@link <target>}` links another doc by identity (`[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`): the CLI prints the command that opens it, and `astryx doctor` warns on one that names no doc.
Preview type for token tables in this section. The CLI rejects a value not in the list below and returns the value in `astryx docs --json`, but draws no preview from it. Omit for non-token sections.
Token category for foundational docs that map to a token section (e.g. 'color'). `astryx docs --json` returns it as authored; no tokens page links to the doc through it.

content.label: A reference doc with one section

content.text: A stamped generic doc without `title`, `description` or `sections` still loads, as older codemod output does; its title falls back to `displayName` or `name`. Without a description and sections it is not a usable topic, and `astryx doctor` reports it.

Each `sections[].content` is an ordered array of ReferenceContentBlock, the stable discriminated union of prose, heading, code, table, list, and token-ref, plus the reference block (ReferenceDocBlock). A read inlines a reference block the way it inlines a token-ref, so `astryx docs`, in text and in `--json`, returns only the stable block kinds. Docs-graph-only workflow and collection blocks are exported separately as GraphContentBlock and accepted by NamespaceDoc. choice, callout, and checklist remain invalid. ReferenceContentBlock is also reused by the `notes` field on SchemaDoc and CommandDoc. Inside text, `{@link <target>}` links another doc by identity (`[<provider>:]<kind>:<name>`): the CLI prints the command that opens it, and `astryx doctor` warns on one that names no doc. Write a CLI command in text, shell code, or a table cell as a bare `astryx` command: a text read adds the runner the reader uses in front of it, and `--json` returns it as written.

A reference block includes content, where a link only points at it: `astryx doctor integration docs` fails when its target names no doc, when `projection.fields` names a field the schema does not have, or when the doc cannot take the projection or presentation it sets, and a read marks the missing content. A target without a provider names a doc of the package that wrote it, so an integration names the CLI's docs with the CLI's provider, as in `@astryxdesign/cli:schema:integration`.

content.label: A section that includes two fields of the integration manifest
ReferenceContentBlock union

content.text: A `token-ref` block (e.g. {type: 'token-ref', topic: 'tokens', section: 'Color Tokens'}) references a token table in another topic; the CLI resolves and inlines it at read time so the docsite can render live theme values.

A section may set `previewType`, a hint for previewing its token table, to one of 'swatch' | 'shadow-box' | 'radius-box' | 'spacing-bar' | 'size-bar' | 'border-line' | 'duration-bar' | 'easing-curve' | 'font-sample'; the CLI rejects any other value.

The doc-type for documenting an authored/received OBJECT shape (astryx.config, a codemod payload, the doc-types themselves). Colocated as a `.doc.mjs` next to the schema it describes. Fields nest recursively, so a whole shape is one tree.
Applies to: <schema>.doc.mjs

rows: Doc-kind discriminant. Marks the file as a schema doc.
URL-safe identifier, used as the docs slug within its namespace. Example: 'config'.

The group that reads this doc: 'authoring' for a file an author writes (a section of {@link generic:field-reference}), or 'cli/api' for a shape the CLI returns (the docs tree adopts it by kind, as the leaf `cli/api/schemas/<name>`). Every schema doc the CLI ships declares one, and `astryx doctor` fails on one that is missing or that nothing reads.
Reserved: alternate slugs for this doc. Nothing reads it yet: `astryx docs` finds a schema doc by its `name` only.
What this schema applies to, e.g. 'astryx.config.{ts,mjs,js}' | 'AstryxConfig'.
The fields that make up the shape. Object-typed fields nest their members recursively via each field's own `fields`, so the whole shape is one tree.
Field name, or a dotted path for a nested field (e.g. 'hooks.postCodemod').
TypeScript type signature as a string, e.g. 'string[]' | "'a' | 'b'".
What the field is for, in 1-2 sentences.
True if the field must be provided. Omit (don't set false) if optional.
Default value as a string, if any.
Deprecation reason, if the field is deprecated.
Nested object fields, for object-typed fields. Recursive.
Optional heading shown above the snippet.

Freeform prose/notes rendered after the field table and examples. The stable ReferenceContentBlock union (prose, heading, code, table, list, token-ref), without the reference block a ReferenceDoc section also takes; a token-ref note is accepted but not rendered.

content.label: A small schema doc with a nested object field

content.text: SchemaFieldDoc is recursive: an object-typed field lists its members in its own `fields`, so an entire nested shape (including paths like `hooks.postCodemod` or `experimental.xle.components`) is documented as one tree.
Name nested fields with a dotted path from the root (e.g. `hooks.postCodemod`) so readers can see where each field sits in the shape.

items: Set `required: true` only for mandatory fields.
Keep `type` close to the real TS type; use single quotes for string-literal unions.
Set `required: false` for optional fields; omit `required` entirely instead.

content.text: The doc-type for template metadata. A discriminated union of PageTemplateDoc (type: 'page') for full page templates and BlockTemplateDoc (type: 'block') for editable compositions. A block can stand alone or use `exampleFor` to attach to one component; `isShowcase` requires that component ownership.
Applies to: <Name>.doc.mjs

rows: Discriminant selecting the variant: 'page' for a full page template, 'block' for an editable composition that may be standalone or component-owned.

Stable identifier for block templates; change `displayName`, not `name`, to edit their visible label in the gallery. For page templates it is a human-readable label, while the existing template-directory/CLI slug owns the default registry path. `astryx template --list` and `astryx search` print `name` as the label of both, and `astryx template <id>` finds a template by its id, never by `name`: an integration template's id is its path under the templates folder without the `.doc.*` suffix.

Human-readable label for the gallery. The CLI prints `name` instead; `astryx template --list --json` also returns an integration template's `displayName`. Spaces out block names that mirror a PascalCase component ('ChatMessageMetadata' → 'Chat Message Metadata').

Optional public registry identity. The converter derives a stable kebab-case slug from `name` (or the existing page-template slug); set `slug` only to override it, and keep prior relative paths in `aliases` after a published rename.
One-sentence description of what the template provides.

Search keywords for CLI discovery: the ideas, domains, and other names a builder might use for what the template serves (e.g. ['monitoring', 'uptime', 'on-call'] for a service-health dashboard). Lowercase. `astryx search` matches them as it matches the description and `astryx build` ranks page templates on them, so keep them out of `description`. Integration templates need @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.6 or later: earlier CLIs reject the field and drop that template, and CLIs before 0.6.4 also hide the package's doc topics.

Integration templates only: the exact id of the Core template this one replaces for unqualified lookup. Find it with `astryx --json template --list --package @astryxdesign/core`; the Core original stays selectable with `--package @astryxdesign/core`. A page replaces only a Core page and a block only a Core block. Needs @astryxdesign/cli 0.6.4 or later: earlier CLIs reject the field, drop that template, and hide the package's doc topics.
Whether the template is ready for use. false shows as '(WIP)' in the gallery and CLI.
Scaffolding-only template (e.g. blank page): available via the CLI but hidden from browsable galleries.
Functional gallery category following a 'Group - Variant' convention (e.g. 'Dashboard - Analytics', 'Table - Basic', 'Form - Wizard'). The overview groups by the text before ' - '.
Opt out of the Templates overview gallery while staying available via the CLI. Use for duplicate/experimental variants. Scaffold templates are hidden automatically.
Block templates only: optional component ownership. Set this when the block is specifically an example of one component. Omit it for a standalone composition.
Block templates only: additional component/hook doc pages whose Examples section should include this block.
Block templates only: additional doc pages whose hero showcase should reuse this block (secondary placements; does not change the primary showcase).
Block templates only (required): width-to-height ratio for preview containers (e.g. 16/9, 1, 3/4).
Block templates only: scale factor for the block preview. Default: 1.
Block templates only: component names this block uses, for 'See also'/'Used in' cross-references (not primary attribution).
Block templates only: when true this block is the canonical hero showcase for its `exampleFor` component. Requires `exampleFor`.

content.label: Page template
Block template (component example)

content.text: When it loads, a template may leave out `displayName` and `aspectRatio` and use its own `category`, as integration templates already published do; a block with no `aspectRatio` previews at 1. Write to the type anyway; it is the contract, and `astryx doctor integration validate` warns about an integration template that leaves out `displayName` or `aspectRatio`.

TemplateDoc is a discriminated union keyed by `type`. Set `type: 'page'` for a full page template. Set `type: 'block'` for an editable composition; add `exampleFor` only when one component owns the example.

items: PageTemplateDoc (type: 'page'): a full page template; `name` doubles as its display value.
BlockTemplateDoc (type: 'block'): an editable composition. `exampleFor` is optional component ownership; omit it for a standalone block. `isShowcase` requires `exampleFor`.

content.text: `category` uses the shared TemplateCategory taxonomy: 'Group - Variant' strings (e.g. 'Table - Bulk Actions'). Not every value maps to an existing template; unused values are reserved so authors get autocomplete for the full taxonomy.
The doc-type for an integration package's template metadata. It has every TemplateDoc field and rule, except that `category` is the package's own string instead of a TemplateCategory value.
Applies to: <Name>.doc.mjs

rows: The package's own category. Bare `astryx template` groups the package's templates by it.

content.label: Block template in an integration package

content.text: Every other field, and the page and block variants, are TemplateDoc's. Core's own templates use TemplateDoc, whose `category` is a TemplateCategory value. `astryx doctor integration validate` checks an integration's template docs against IntegrationTemplateDoc.
The strongly typed descriptor for one source theme: bundled with the CLI, shipped by an integration, or kept in the project's src/themes, where `theme eject` writes one.
Applies to: <theme-source-stem>.doc.mjs

rows: Lower-kebab CLI theme identity. Must match the descriptor parent directory. Example: 'ocean'.
Human-readable name shown by theme listings. Example: 'Ocean'.
One-line summary shown by theme listings.
Whether the owning package actively maintains this theme.

content.label: A theme descriptor beside oceanTheme.ts

content.text: ThemeDoc is static metadata. The descriptor holds one default-exported object of literal string and boolean fields, directly under a `/** @type {import('@astryxdesign/cli/authoring').ThemeDoc} */` comment, and nothing else: without that comment, or with any other statement, it fails to load. Discovery validates it without executing the descriptor or theme source.
The descriptor and source share one stem. For oceanTheme.doc.mjs, discovery requires exactly one oceanTheme source module and a named oceanTheme runtime export.
The parent theme directory, including this descriptor, is the complete copy and pack boundary. Nested source, palettes, assets, and receipts need no second file list.

docs.name: font-setup
docs.title: Font Setup
docs.description: Font families, custom font loading, geometric font sizes, and semantic font weights.

content.text: Typography is built on a geometric type scale: base size × ratio^step, with 14px and 1.2 as defaults. Every text style is a semantic token that composes font size, weight, and line-height, so components express intent (heading, body, label) rather than raw values.

Two layers work together: raw size tokens (--font-size-xs ... --font-size-5xl) form the geometric scale, and semantic type scale tokens (--text-heading-1-size, --text-body-leading, etc.) reference them by var(). Themes override the entire scale by adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme; all semantic tokens recompute automatically.

Three font roles: body (UI text), heading (titles and headings), and code (monospace). By default, body and heading share the same system font stack; code uses a monospace stack. Custom themes can assign different families per role; heading inherits from body when not explicitly set.

Astryx never loads font files. defineTheme and the built CSS only set font-family: naming a webfont (Fraunces, JetBrains Mono, and so on) makes every browser look for it, and quietly fall back when the app has not loaded it. `{@command theme build}` warns when a theme names families that are neither CSS generics nor common system fonts and prints the snippet to add; loading the font is always the app's job.

content.label: Google Fonts: add to your document <head>
content.code:
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Fraunces:wght@400;600;700&family=JetBrains+Mono&display=swap"
/>

content.label: Self-hosted: one @font-face per family and weight

content.text: Always pair a webfont with a real fallback stack (metric-similar system fonts plus a generic) so text stays readable before the font loads and wherever it never does: defineTheme({typography: {heading: {family: 'Fraunces', fallbacks: 'Georgia, serif'}}}).

Geometric scale: round(base × ratio^step), expressed in rem. The default scale is 14px × 1.2, producing 12 steps from 4xs (6px) to 5xl (42px). Adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme regenerates every size token while preserving proportional relationships.

Four semantic weights: normal (400, body/code), medium (500, labels/data), semibold (600, headings/titles), bold (700, strong emphasis). Type scale tokens reference these by var() so themes can remap numeric values.

docs.name: fonts-and-assets
docs.title: Fonts and assets
docs.description: Name the fonts in the theme, then export an optional font stylesheet that `theme add` imports with the built theme.

content.text: A theme names its typefaces in `typography`: `body`, `heading`, and `code`, each with a `family` and `fallbacks`. These set the `--font-family-*` tokens every component reads. Always give real `fallbacks` so text stays readable before the font loads, or if it never does. `heading` inherits `family` and `fallbacks` from `body` when you omit them.
The full type scale and font roles are in {@link generic:author-a-theme}.

Naming a family does not load it. When the theme uses non-system fonts, add `<slug>.fonts.css` beside the built module and production CSS, then export it as `./themes/<slug>.fonts.css`. `theme add` imports that stylesheet with the built theme.

The stylesheet can contain self-hosted `@font-face` rules or import a hosted stylesheet. A hosted `@import` is simple, but it delays loading compared with a preconnected `<link>`; choose that trade-off deliberately. Doctor warns when it cannot prove the loader — a hosted `@import`, or no font stylesheet while the app loads the family itself — but the warning does not fail the app.

items: Load every weight and style the theme uses. Do not let the browser synthesize bold or italic.
Include self-hosted font files and their licenses in the packed package.
Keep CSS and font assets side-effectful so a bundler does not remove the loader.
Run `integration verify`; it fails when an exported font stylesheet cannot resolve, but it does not check the font files the stylesheet names.

content.text: Before publishing, run `integration verify`. Then install the package in a clean app, run `theme add`, apply the generated theme, and open it in a browser. The source, packed exports, and applied result form one chain; check the last step too.

items: Text renders in the named families at every weight and style — the italic face resolves, not a synthesized slant.
Every font request succeeds; nothing silently falls back to a system font.
Color pairs still meet contrast in both light and dark mode.

docs.name: generate-a-palette
docs.title: Generate a palette
docs.description: Turn a few seed colors into full light and dark color ramps, saved in the theme folder.

content.text: A theme needs dozens of related colors — shades of each brand color for backgrounds, borders, text, and states, in both light and dark mode. A palette is that full set of shades. Rather than hand-pick every one, you name a few seed colors and generate the rest, so the shades stay consistent.

You write a short config naming each color family and its seed, then run `theme palette generate`. It expands each seed into a full light and dark ramp — the scale of shades — and writes the result into the theme folder, where your theme tokens point at it (see {@link generic:define-the-theme}). Keep the config and the generated palette together in that folder.
The smallest config is one color family: an `id` to name it and a `seed` color to grow it from. Save it as `themes/ocean/palette.config.json`:

content.code: {"families": [{"id": "ocean", "seed": "#0074e2"}]}

# Print the palette without writing files
{@command theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json}
# Write the palette and its receipt
astryx theme palette generate themes/ocean/palette.config.json \
  --out themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.ts

[ok] Wrote themes/ocean/tokens/ocean.palette.receipt.json

Review and edit the candidate before adopting it as theme-owned palette data.

content.text: The command writes two files. `ocean.palette.ts` is the palette your theme tokens will read: it exports `black`, `white`, and `palette` — a ramp of 21 shades (stops `0` to `100`) for both `light` and `dark`. The `.receipt.json` beside it records the exact seeds and settings, so you can regenerate the same palette later. A second run leaves both files alone unless you pass `--overwrite`.

Add `--preview <file>.html` to also get a web page showing every shade, so you can eyeball the palette in a browser. Write it outside `themes/` so it does not ship in your package. Every option is in {@link command:theme palette generate}, and the config it reads is described in {@link function:generateTonalPalette}.

docs.name: global-integrations
docs.title: Make your integration work globally
docs.description: People can install your integration next to their global Astryx install, where it works in every folder outside a project; inside a project, only the project's own integrations work. A checklist, with the exact commands to try it.

sections.title: First: your peer ranges must include the global CLI's version

content.text: Your `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` ranges must include the version of the CLI installed globally. If they do not, Astryx skips your package outside projects, and `{@command doctor}` warns and names the range.
Inside a project that does not install your package, `{@command discover}` offers it, with the command that adds it to that project, once your peer range admits the project's release.

items: Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`{@pm install @astryxdesign/cli your-package --global}`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `{@command discover}` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.

content.text: Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.

items: Declare the `@astryxdesign/core` (and, if you use it, `@astryxdesign/cli`) `peerDependencies` range your package really supports. Outside a project, Astryx skips your package when that range leaves out the global version, and `{@command doctor}` says why: too narrow, and global users lose it after an upgrade; too wide, and it loads against a Core it may not build with.
Keep imports in your docs and templates to packages an app installs with yours, since outside a project there is no app to check them against.

If you set `cliCommand`, know that outside a project it starts every command Astryx prints, and that two global integrations naming different commands cancel out, falling back to `astryx` ({@link generic:cli-command}). Inside an app, only the app's integrations count.
Try it globally before you publish, with the steps below.

content.text: Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:

items: `{@command discover}` lists your package as installed, with what it adds.
`{@command docs}` lists your topics, and `{@command search <one of your component names>}` finds them.
`{@command doctor}`'s `computer-integrations` check lists your package as used, with no warning.
In an app that does not install it, `{@command discover}` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command, and none of its components or docs show up.

content.text: Remove it again with `{@pm remove your-package --global}`.
How global mode works for the people who install your package: {@link namespace:global}. Their side of global integrations: {@link generic:computer-integrations}.

docs.name: global
docs.title: Global mode
docs.summary: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.

blocks.text: Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
What you get

items: Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.

blocks.text: Which version runs

rows: The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only `@astryxdesign/core`, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Commands for your computer, such as `{@command init --user}`
Your global version, in any folder.

blocks.text: Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: {@link generic:project-global-or-both}. The details: {@link generic:who-answers}.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: {@link generic:updates}.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: {@link generic:computer-agent-guide}.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: {@link generic:computer-integrations}. Building one: {@link generic:global-integrations}.
More

items: Install, and work offline: {@link generic:install-once}.
Monorepos and nested folders: {@link generic:monorepos}.
CI and containers: {@link generic:ci-and-containers}.
Something looks wrong: {@link generic:problems}.
Uninstall and reset: {@link generic:uninstall}.
Every path, setting, JSON field, and error code: {@link generic:reference}.
What each command does outside a project: {@link namespace:commands}.

docs.name: grade-template-with-agent
docs.title: Grade and improve with an agent
docs.description: Give an agent the rubric and evidence it needs to find problems, produce a reproducible scorecard, and improve the template.

content.text: Grade one exact package revision against template rubric 1.4. Give the agent the template id, the package name, and a clean app that can install the packed package, then use this prompt. Replace every angle-bracket value. The first pass is read-only so the original score and findings stay visible.

content.label: Agent grading prompt
content.code:
Grade integration template <id> from <package> at <revision>.

Before scoring:
1. Read `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates --full`.
2. Read `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates/template-grading-rubric --full` and every guide it links.
3. Inspect the template source, its matching .doc.mjs file, package.json exports and files, and astryx.integration.mjs.
4. Run `astryx integration verify` in the package.
5. Follow `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/package-and-test/test-template-in-app --full`: install the packed package in the clean app, copy the template, build the app, and render the behavior matrix.

Score all seven rubric categories. Cite file and line evidence for every deduction. Do not award points for a state you did not inspect. If browser or build evidence is unavailable, say so and mark the template not publishable.

Return the rubric version, package revision, numeric score, letter grade, category scorecard, publishable yes/no verdict, detailed findings, and the top three fixes. Treat 100 as the target. Name every remaining deduction and say whether it is an intentional tradeoff or still needs work. Do not edit files during this first pass.

# Template grade: <id>

**Rubric:** 1.4
**Package revision:** <revision>
**Type:** page | block
**Grade:** <letter> (<score>/100)
**Publishable:** yes | no

| Category | Points | Max | Evidence |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Astryx component purity | X | 30 | |
| Icon purity | X | 15 | |
| Custom CSS | X | 15 | |
| Layout & structure | X | 15 | |
| Doc metadata | X | 10 | |
| Image handling | X | 5 | |
| Code quality | X | 10 | |
| **Total** | **X** | **100** | |

## Detailed findings
- <file:line, rubric rule, observed problem, and deduction>

## Publication blockers
- <failed pack, copy, build, asset, browser, theme, responsive, or input check>

## Top three fixes
1. <highest-value fix>
2. <second fix>
3. <third fix>

content.text: The category scores must add exactly to the total, and the grade comes from the published bands. The verdict is `yes` only when the score is 75 or higher and every package, copy, build, asset, and rendered-app check passes.

items: Fix publication blockers first.
Fix every reasonable deduction without hiding it behind helper components or package CSS.
Pack again, copy into a fresh app, and have the agent repeat the full grade. Keep the earlier scorecard so the improvement is visible.
Stop only when no reasonable fix remains, and record every intentional tradeoff that still costs points.

docs.name: headers-and-footers
docs.title: Headers and footers
docs.description: Pin a header or footer while the body scrolls, so the title and commit actions stay reachable.

content.text: A region can pin a header or footer while its body scrolls. Both are Layout slots, and padding set once on Layout reaches all three, so header, body, and footer share one content line.

items: LayoutHeader in the header slot: the region title and its primary action
Toolbar instead of LayoutHeader when the header carries interactive controls
LayoutFooter in the footer slot: actions that commit the work and must stay reachable
defaultHasDividers on Layout fences both at once, rather than hasDivider per slot

content.label: Pinned header and footer around a scrolling body

content.text: Verify: scroll the body. The header and footer stay put, their dividers run full-bleed, and all three still share one left content line.

docs.name: help
docs.title: Help
docs.summary: Find a CLI message and how to fix it.

docs.name: host-entry
docs.title: Host entry
docs.description: Run the Astryx CLI from your own command-line tool: the inputs `runHostedCli` takes, what it returns, and when the process ends instead.

content.text: A tool that carries the CLI for its own users starts one run per process with `runHostedCli` from `@astryxdesign/cli/host`. The run behaves as the CLI's own command does with the same arguments in the same folder, and the commands it prints start with your tool's command.

rows: The command-line arguments, without the command name.
The folder the run works in. It must exist.
The command your users type, such as `acme astryx`: a non-blank single line of at most 120 characters, with no surrounding spaces.
Why you did not run the project's own CLI, such as `untrusted`: a non-blank single line of at most 120 characters. That CLI then never runs.

Your package sets, in order of preference: folders whose `node_modules` each hold a CLI, the Core of the same release, and integrations. A run never installs a release; it takes the release a project needs from the first set that holds it.
Integrations you approve for use outside a project, by package name.
Your own discover sources. `{@command discover}` reports each as the host's.

items: It resolves with `{status, packages}`: the exit status the CLI's own command would exit with, and each package the run used, with its version and whether it came from the project or a package set.
When another release answers from one of your package sets through its own host entry, that entry runs in the same process with the same inputs, and the call resolves with its result.
It rejects with a `TypeError`, before anything runs, for an unknown option or an invalid value, and with an `Error` when a run already started in the process. Start each run in a new process.

content.text: Like the CLI's own command, a run ends the process with its exit status, and the call never resolves, when it:

items: prints help or the version (`--help`, `-h`, `help`, `--version`, `-V`, `--version --json`);
rejects the command line, such as an unknown command or option;
reports an error it stops on, including every error in `--json` mode;
meets an unexpected error;
hands the run to another CLI's own command: the project's CLI when you pass no `declinedProjectCli`, or a package set whose CLI has no host entry.

docs.name: i18n-calendars
docs.title: Other calendars
docs.description: Show dates in the Persian, Hebrew, Islamic, Buddhist, Japanese, and other calendars while values stay Gregorian ISO dates.

content.text: Set `calendar` on `<InternationalizationProvider>` for a subtree, or on `Calendar` itself; without it, `Calendar` is Gregorian. Values stay Gregorian ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`) in every calendar.

content.label: Persian dates in a Persian interface

content.text: Most calendars need the runtime's `Temporal`. Safari and older runtimes lack it: load `temporal-polyfill/full/global` there, on the server and in the browser. Without it, those calendars show Gregorian dates. See {@link namespace:calendars} for the supported calendars, server rendering, and the lunisolar calendars.

docs.name: i18n-library-integration
docs.title: Library Integration
docs.description: Override astryx's default text, coexist with react-intl / i18next / next-intl / LinguiJS, or use astryx as your i18n library.

content.text: Use `overrides` to change individual strings without shipping a full catalog. Overrides are keyed by locale and merged on top of the built-in and user-supplied catalogs.

content.label: Change one string in English
content.code:
<InternationalizationProvider
  locale="en"
  overrides={{en: {'@astryx.pagination.next': 'Next →'}}}
>
  <App />
</InternationalizationProvider>

content.text: Overrides win over both bundled English and any `messages` catalog for the same key. Use them for brand voice tweaks or one-off wording changes.

sections.title: Using astryx with your own i18n library

content.text: Astryx components render astryx strings through astryx's provider. Consumer components render consumer strings through whatever i18n library you already use: react-intl, i18next, next-intl, LinguiJS, and so on. The two systems coexist and read from the same source of truth for the active locale.

content.label: Astryx + react-intl side by side

content.text: Keep the two providers in sync on locale, and each library owns its own catalog. Astryx never sees your app strings, and your i18n library never sees astryx internals. Runtime locale swap works the same way: re-render both providers with a new `locale` prop and the whole tree updates live.

Single-catalog usage (where an external i18n runtime like react-intl or i18next resolves both your app strings AND astryx's strings through one provider) is on the roadmap via a `Translator` adapter. Track [meta/astryx#4029](https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/4029). For now, run the two providers side by side as shown above.

sections.title: Using astryx as your i18n library

content.text: For production apps with substantial localization needs, we recommend a dedicated i18n library such as react-intl, i18next, next-intl, or LinguiJS. If your app is small or you do not want another runtime, you can resolve your own strings through astryx too. Keep app keys in a separate namespace from `@astryx.*`, and include your own `en` catalog because astryx's built-in English fallback only contains astryx component strings.

content.label: Translate app strings with astryx

content.text: `Catalog` types the rich `{defaultMessage, description?}` authoring shape. `RuntimeCatalog` types the generated key-to-message string map. `ProviderMessagesByLocale` accepts either shape for the provider, while `MessagesByLocale` keeps the original rich-only context shape.

docs.name: i18n-quick-start
docs.title: Quick Start
docs.description: Wrap your app in InternationalizationProvider, load a locale catalog, and swap languages at runtime.

content.text: Internationalization ships with `@astryxdesign/core`. There is nothing to install. Wrap your app in `<InternationalizationProvider>` and set the active `locale`; astryx components pick up localized strings from that provider.

content.label: Wrap your app

content.text: The provider always has the built-in English catalog. Pass additional catalogs through `messages` when you enable another locale.

content.label: Load an astryx locale catalog

content.text: Astryx ships English and first-party translations for supported locales. Compact runtime modules from `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.generated.js` contain only the messages apps need; the existing `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.json` files retain translator context. Until a locale is available, apps can pass a local catalog in either shape. Missing keys fall back through the locale chain to English (for example, `pt-BR` walks to `pt`, then to shipped `en`).
Locale catalogs only affect astryx strings. Your app can continue using its own i18n system for product copy.
Re-render `<InternationalizationProvider>` with a new `locale` prop and every astryx string updates live. No reload, no separate API call.

content.label: Toggle between locales

content.text: Persisting the user's choice (localStorage, cookie, URL segment, account setting) is up to the consumer. Astryx reads whatever `locale` you pass in.

docs.name: i18n-rtl-and-testing
docs.title: RTL & Testing
docs.description: Text direction (RTL), pseudo-locale testing, and contributor guidance for developers and translators.

content.text: Astryx tracks text direction (`'ltr'` or `'rtl'`) alongside the locale. By default the direction is derived from the `locale` you pass to `<InternationalizationProvider>` via [`Intl.Locale.getTextInfo()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Locale/getTextInfo), so RTL locales such as Arabic (`ar`), Hebrew (`he`), Farsi (`fa`), and Urdu (`ur`) resolve to `'rtl'` automatically.

You don't wire anything per component. Once the direction is set, astryx components mirror on their own: layout and spacing flip via CSS logical properties, directional icons (chevrons, carets) flip in place, keyboard arrow keys swap left/right, and overlays position on the correct side. Set the direction once and the whole component tree follows.

content.label: Direction derived from locale

content.text: Pass the optional `dir` prop to force a direction. This overrides the locale-derived default; useful for RTL layout testing under an English catalog, or to skip derivation when you already know the direction.

content.label: Explicit direction override

content.text: There's one more step: tell the browser about the direction too. Add a `dir` attribute to your page; usually on the `<html>` tag. This is what makes text align to the correct side, punctuation and mixed-language text flow correctly, and layouts mirror. The provider handles astryx components; the `dir` attribute handles everything else on the page.

Astryx doesn't set `dir` for you; you set it, alongside the same direction you pass to the provider. If your app is server-rendered (like Next.js), the `getLocaleDirection()` helper computes the direction from a locale so you can set it while the page renders:

content.label: Set <html dir> in a Next.js root layout

content.text: In a plain client app, set the same attribute on `<html>` whenever the locale changes. (`getLocaleDirection()` safely returns `'ltr'` for anything it doesn't recognize, so you can call it with any locale string.)

To make just one part of a left-to-right page right-to-left; say an Arabic quote or a comment thread; wrap that part in its own `<InternationalizationProvider dir="rtl">` and add `dir="rtl"` to the element around it. Pop-up overlays; menus, dialogs, popovers, tooltips; opened from inside that region mirror too: they position with logical CSS anchor placement, so they land on the correct side and inherit the region's direction automatically.

Astryx generates a `pseudo` locale that wraps every string in `⟦…⟧` and replaces letters with accented look-alikes. Turn it on in development to catch hardcoded astryx strings and layout issues caused by longer text.

content.label: Turn on pseudo-localization

content.text: Developers
Astryx component authors read strings with `useTranslator()` rather than hardcoding user-facing text.

content.label: Read an astryx string

content.text: Astryx's own strings live in `packages/core/locales/en.json`. New user-facing strings must go through `useTranslator`; this is enforced by the `@astryx/no-hardcoded-i18n-string` ESLint rule. See the AI contribution guide for the alias-and-resolve pattern used when adding new keys.
When you author a component that needs to respond to direction, resolve it from the DOM, not from a render-time JavaScript read, and reach for the lightest tool that works. In priority order:
1. CSS logical properties first

Use `insetInlineStart`, `paddingInlineEnd`, `marginInline`, and friends instead of physical `left`/`right`. Most mirroring needs nothing more; the browser flips it from the ambient `dir`. The `@astryx/no-physical-properties` ESLint rule enforces this.
2. Directional icons: mirror with CSS, not a name-swap

Render one fixed glyph and wrap it in the shared `rtlStyles.mirror` (a `scaleX(-1)` that only applies under `[dir="rtl"]`). It flips from the ancestor `dir` through the cascade, so it works on the server with no hydration flash. Do not pick `chevronLeft` vs `chevronRight` in JS. This is how Pagination, Calendar, and Carousel handle their chevrons.

content.label: Mirror a directional icon with CSS

content.text: 3. Behavioral logic: read the DOM lazily, on the event

For things CSS can't express; keyboard arrow-key mapping, drag/scroll math; read direction at interaction time with `isRtlElement(el)` (a `getComputedStyle().direction` check), never during render. The focus primitives (`useListFocus`, `useGridFocus`, `useTreeFocus`) already auto-detect direction from their container, so arrow keys flip for free; don't pass a direction flag to them.
4. useDirection() context: the last resort

Reach for it only when you genuinely need the direction value during render and none of the above fit. It's SSR-safe and returns `'ltr'` outside a provider (matching `useTranslator`'s silent fallback), but it's the one path that can mismatch on hydration if the provider's `direction` disagrees with `<html dir>`; so prefer the options above, which resolve purely from the DOM. As of the CSS-mirror migration, no astryx component reads direction from context at render time.
Translators

Crowdin is the preferred way to contribute; [join a language](https://crowdin.com/project/astryx), translate strings in the web UI, and your work syncs back to the repo without opening a PR. Direct PRs against `packages/core/locales/*.json` also work if you prefer that flow.

docs.name: icon-definitions
docs.title: Icon definitions
docs.summary: Every icon definition: what an icon stands for, and the shared name icon sets map their icons to.

blocks.text: An icon definition is one thing an icon stands for, such as `close` or `delete`. Every icon set registers its icons against definitions in its data file's `map`, and templates are written against definitions, so a project that switches icon sets gets the same definition from the new set. Built-in definitions, marked [built-in], are the shared names Core renders (the semantic icon names in `astryx docs icons`); every set maps them, and `integration check` fails until it does. The others are optional: map each one your library draws. `map` keys a definition by its camelCase name, shown after the id (`eyeSlash`); `experimental icon map` and `--pairs` take either spelling. A set may add its own definitions; in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`, they are listed here with the package that ships them. `astryx experimental icon <definition>` finds the icon each installed set draws for it. Icon definitions are experimental: they may change or be removed in a patch release.

docs.name: icon-set-files
docs.title: Icon set files
docs.description: Every field of the files an icon set is made of: the descriptor, the data file, and an icon definition.

content.text: Experimental: may change or be removed in a patch release. The strongly typed descriptor for one icon set an integration ships: what a person writes about the set. The set's icons, and what each one means, live in the `<name>.icons.json` data file beside it.
Applies to: <iconSetsRoot>/<name>/<name>.doc.mjs

rows: Lower-kebab icon-set identity. Must match the descriptor parent directory. Example: 'outline'.
Human-readable name shown by `astryx experimental icon --list`. Example: 'Acme Outline'.
One-line summary shown by `astryx experimental icon --list`.
Whether the owning package actively maintains this set.
SPDX license expression for the artwork. Example: 'MIT'.

content.label: An icon-set descriptor at icons/outline/outline.doc.mjs

content.text: Point the manifest's `experimental.iconSets` field at the folder that holds your sets. Each lower-kebab folder under it is one set, named by the folder, and holds `<name>.doc.mjs`, `<name>.icons.json`, and any license notice files. The manifest never lists sets or icons.

Write the descriptor as one default-exported object of literal strings and booleans under a `/** @type {import('@astryxdesign/cli/authoring').IconSetDoc} */` comment, with nothing else in the file. Discovery reads it, and the data file, without executing them or the icon module.

The data file is described by {@link schema:icon-set-data}. Run `astryx integration check` to prove every export it names exists in the module and that the theme map agrees with the built-in entries of `map`.

Experimental: may change or be removed in a patch release. An icon set's data file: which icons exist, the export that draws each one, the words a person might search for, and which icon draws each icon definition (`map`). `astryx experimental icon`, template icon mapping, and the checks read this file and nothing else.
Applies to: <iconSetsRoot>/<name>/<name>.icons.json

rows: The import specifier every `export` is read from: the set's own package name, or one of its package.json `exports` subpaths. Never a file path. Example: '@acme/outline-icons'.
The upstream library and version the file was generated from. Omit it for a set with no upstream.

Library exports that are not icons. `experimental icon new-set --from` leaves them out every time it wraps or refreshes the set; `--exclude` adds to the list. A CLI whose reference does not list this key withdraws a set that sets it, naming the key; leave it out for a set those CLIs must read.

The module `astryx experimental icon add` writes, as a `./` path from the package root: one export per icon, a re-export of a library component or the adapter applied to a library export, and `themeIcons`, the theme map, from the built-in entries of `map`. The CLI writes its declaration file beside it. The package's entry re-exports it. Example: './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js'.

A function in the package, `(source) => Component`, that turns a library export that is not a component (icon data, an SVG string or URL) into one. `module` is a `./` path from the package root. Example: {module: './src/adapt.js', export: 'adapt'}.
The named looks the set offers, in lower-kebab case, such as `outline` and `solid`. Icon size is never a variant: CSS sets it. Omit it when the set has one look. Example: ['outline', 'solid'].
The variant each icon's own `export` draws; one of `variants`. Example: {variant: 'outline'}.
The export that maps each built-in icon definition to its artwork, keyed by exactly the built-in definitions in `map`. Example: 'themeIcons'.

Which of this set's icons draws each icon definition: definition name to icon `id`. Keys are Astryx's definitions (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions`) or ones the set declares in its `definitions` folder, one file per definition. One icon may draw several definitions; each definition maps to one icon. Every built-in definition must be mapped. Example: {"close": "x", "delete": "trash", "remove": "trash"}.
Lower-kebab identity, unique in the set. Example: 'trash'.
The named export that draws the icon's default variant, named `<Name>Icon`: a React component that takes SVG props and draws with `currentColor`. Example: 'TrashIcon'.
The import specifier, when it differs from the set's `module`.

Lower-case terms a person might search for, the words of the icon's own name included; at least one. Do not copy the words of the definitions `map` names the icon for: search already matches the icon by them. Example: ['trash', 'delete', 'remove', 'bin'].
Other variants of the icon: each names one of `variants`, never the default, and the export that draws it. At most one export per variant.

Reviewed equivalents of this icon in other icon sets or libraries, such as `{set: 'lines', export: 'CrossIcon', variant: 'solid', confidence: 'exact'}`. When a copied template imports a matched icon from that installed set, `exact` and `strong` matches are used before any other rule; a `likely` match is only suggested. A match never names this set itself.

content.label: A data file at icons/outline/outline.icons.json
content.code:
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "module": "@acme/outline-icons",
  "generated": "./icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js",
  "variants": ["outline", "solid"],
  "default": {"variant": "outline"},
  "themeMap": "themeIcons",
  "map": {"close": "x", "delete": "trash"},
  "icons": [
    {"id": "x", "export": "XIcon", "words": ["close", "cancel", "dismiss"]},
    {
      "id": "trash",
      "export": "TrashIcon",
      "words": ["trash", "delete", "remove", "bin"],
      "variants": [{"variant": "solid", "export": "TrashSolidIcon"}]
    }
  ]
}

content.text: A file that fails this schema, repeats an id, gives an icon no words, has a `map` key that is not camelCase or a `map` value that is not an icon id in the file, or names a variant `variants` does not declare is invalid, and its set is withdrawn from every surface until it is fixed. `astryx doctor` names the reason.

A template declares the icon definition each icon it imports draws. With a project icon set, each declared icon maps to the icon whose `matches` name it with `exact` or `strong` confidence (for an icon another installed set ships), else to the icon this file's `map` names for its definition. Nothing is guessed from names or words.

Write it with the CLI: `astryx experimental icon add` registers one icon and its `map` entry, `astryx experimental icon map` changes an entry, and `astryx experimental icon new-set --from` wraps a whole library.

Experimental: may change or be removed in a patch release. One thing an icon can stand for, such as `close` or `delete`. Astryx ships one file per definition; an icon set adds its own in the same format. A set's data file `map` registers which of its icons draws each definition.
Applies to: <iconSetsRoot>/<set>/definitions/<name>.doc.mjs

rows: camelCase identity: the key a data file's `map` uses. Must match the file name. Example: 'delete'.
One sentence: what an icon with this definition is for. Example: 'Delete something permanently.'.
Lower-case terms a person might search for; at least one. Example: ['trash', 'bin', 'discard'].
Only on Astryx's own definitions: the definition is a shared icon name Core renders, so every icon set maps it.
Marks the definition as experimental: the icon-definitions listing shows it as `[experimental]`. Omit it for a definition you mean to keep.

content.label: A set's own definition at icon-sets/outline/definitions/random.doc.mjs

content.text: A set's own definitions sit in a `definitions` folder in the set's directory, one file per definition. Its `map` registers icons for them like for Astryx's. `astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions` lists every definition: Astryx's, and, in a project that sets `experimental.iconSet`, those of each installed set. A definition file refuses a field it does not know.

IconDefinitionDoc is static metadata: one default-exported object of literal fields directly under a `/** @type {import('@astryxdesign/cli/authoring').IconDefinitionDoc} */` comment. Discovery reads it without executing it.
To share a definition with every set, copy its file into Astryx's definitions folder in a pull request.

docs.name: icon-sets
docs.title: Icon sets
docs.description: Ship an icon set: register each icon against an icon definition, so apps find icons by meaning and templates use your icons.

content.text: Icon sets are experimental: the `astryx experimental icon` commands, the `experimental.iconSet` key in astryx.config, the `experimental.iconSets` key in an integration manifest, the data file, icon definitions, and the output and JSON of all of them can change, or go away, in any patch release without a deprecation period. A project that does not set `experimental.iconSet` sees no change in any stable command, apart from: the marked `experimental` group in help and in `astryx manifest` (its command, and its `responseTypes` and `jsonSupported` entries); the marked experimental entries in the CLI reference listings; and a search for "experimental", which also finds the stable `stability` field of the field reference. Templates, discover, and doctor answer as they do with no icon set installed. With a package that ships icon sets installed and no opt-in, the warnings an older CLI gives about the manifest key `experimental` (in `astryx doctor` and `astryx doctor integration validate <package>`, and the one-line nudge other commands print to stderr) are gone. `astryx search` never returns icons or these docs; to find an icon by meaning, use `astryx experimental icon <words>`.

Astryx keeps a list of icon definitions: one file per meaning, like `close` or `delete` (`astryx docs cli/experimental/icon-definitions`). An icon set registers which of its icons draws each definition, in the `map` of its data file; one icon may draw several definitions (`file` and `document` can both be your `document` icon). Templates say which definition each of their icons draws, so a project that uses your set gets your icon for every definition you map. Every set maps the built-in definitions, the names Core renders itself.
The CLI knows no icon library. You, or your agent, pick each icon from the library you wrap; the commands below verify it, write the files, and check the set.

content.code: astryx experimental icon new-set outline

content.text: `outline.doc.mjs` is the descriptor: name, display name and description (`--display-name`, `--description`), and `license`, the SPDX license of the artwork (it starts as your package's own). `outline.icons.json` starts with no icons and an empty `map`; its `module` is your package name. `outline.generated.js` is the set's generated module, with its declaration file `outline.generated.d.ts`: the CLI writes both, and every icon and the theme map are exports of it. Every field is in {@link schema:icon-set-doc} and {@link schema:icon-set-data}.

The set's icons import from your package by name, so your package's entry must re-export the generated module. The command writes only the set's own files: your entry, `exports`, `main`, `types`, `files`, peers, and scripts are yours, and the receipt names each change to make as text to copy. For an entry file in the package (and the declaration file package.json names) that is the line `export * from './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js';`, relative to it; for a package with no entry, `index.js` and `index.d.ts` with that line and the package.json `main`, `types`, and `exports` that name them; for a built or CommonJS entry, the line to add to the source it is built from. `integration check` names the same change until you make it, and the receipt also names the peers and the `typecheck` script to add. `integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files with your package's TypeScript; the receipt says when it is missing (`npm install -D typescript@6`).

sections.title: Add icons one at a time

content.text: Pick an icon from the library and ask which definitions fit it. Nothing is written yet. To read every icon a set already has, one line each with its words and the definitions it draws, run `astryx experimental icon --set <set> --all-icons`; `astryx experimental icon <set>/<id>` reads one, or says the id does not exist:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library

content.text: Each row is an Astryx definition (or one your set declares) with the exact command that adds the icon for it. Run one:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library --definition delete

content.text: The CLI reads the library's exports without running them and refuses a name the module does not export, suggesting close names. It adds the icon as `BinIcon` (id `bin`, words from its name), writes `export {Bin as BinIcon} from '@acme/glyph-library';` to the set's generated module, and sets `map.delete = "bin"`. Running it again changes nothing. Do not copy the definition's words into the icon: `astryx experimental icon` matches an icon by its own words and by the name and words of every definition it is mapped to.
When no Astryx definition fits, add your own in the same command. It needs no pull request:

content.code: astryx experimental icon add Dice5 --from @acme/glyph-library --new-definition random --description 'Pick something at random.' --words dice,shuffle,chance

content.text: `experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` points a definition at an icon the set already has (a definition is named in camelCase, `eyeSlash`, or by the kebab id the definitions list shows, `eye-slash`; an icon by its id, its export name in any case, or another name its library exports it as, such as `trash-2`, never by one word of its id), `experimental icon map --pairs close=x-mark,search=magnifying-glass` writes many entries at once (checked together, all or none; an entry the map already has is replaced, and the receipt shows what it was), and `--remove` drops an entry. `experimental icon new-definition <name> --description ... --words ... --icon <id>` adds your own definition for an icon you already have. `experimental icon --definitions` lists every Astryx definition, built in or not, with its words (`--json` for a script).

content.code: astryx experimental icon new-set outline --from @acme/glyph-library

content.text: Every component the library exports becomes an icon (an alias of one component is recorded once), named `<Name>Icon`, with an id from its name (`Squares2X2Icon` is `squares-2x2`: a dimension stays one word). `map` is filled only where a definition's name is an icon's id (`delete` → icon `delete`), and the receipt lists those entries under Mapped by name: a library can draw another meaning under the same name (one library's `delete` is a backspace key), so check each. An icon whose id is only one of a definition's words (`trash` for `delete`) may mean something else in this library, so the receipt lists it under Suggestions, with the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon>` command for each, and writes nothing for it: check the meaning, then run the ones that fit. Run it again after a library release to refresh the icons that library supplies; `map` entries whose icon still exists are kept, and the receipt names any icon the library dropped, any icon `--exclude` left out, and the `map` entries each took with it. Icons you added from your own files or another library are left as they are. Icons you added one file at a time from the same package (`--from <package>/dist/XIcon`) move to the root import when you refresh from the package root and the root exports the same icon; each keeps its id, export, `map` entries, variants, and words on that refresh and every later one, and the receipt lists it under `moved`. A library icon whose id or name a moved icon already has is left out. When another icon of the set already reads the same root export, the icon stays on its own file, and the receipt says why. An icon you already have is known by the library export it re-exports, so it keeps its export name exactly, its `map` entries, variants, and words, even when a newer CLI spells its id differently or your `--exclude` lets a library prefix come off new ids; the receipt lists each changed id under `renamed`. An id you chose that is not a spelling of the library name (`dismiss` for `XIcon`) is kept. A refresh with `--dry-run` writes nothing and prints the Mapped by name and Suggestions lists again; `--display-name` and `--description` on a refresh rewrite the descriptor. Variants added with `add --variant … --all` are kept too; run that `add` again to pick up icons the release added. `experimental icon --list` shows how many definitions the set maps.

With a package or package subpath, it also records the installed library and version as the data file's `source`, so `integration check` warns when your dependency moves to another version; copies the library's LICENSE (and NOTICE) files into the set directory; and sets the descriptor's `license` to the library's. A set you started without `--from` gets the same the first time a refresh records its source, unless you already changed `license`: a `license` you set is kept (the receipt names the library's), and every later refresh keeps it too. Your package.json `license` is never changed. Edit `license` when the artwork's license differs from the library's package license. When the library ships no license file to copy, the receipt says so under `licenseNoticeMissing` and in its notes, and the CLI writes nothing: add a `NOTICE` file to the set directory (`icon-sets/<set>/NOTICE`) that names the library, its version, and its license. `integration check` accepts a file named `LICENSE`, `LICENCE`, `NOTICE`, or `COPYING`, in any case and with an optional suffix such as `NOTICE.md` or `LICENSE-MIT`, in the set directory or the package root; without one it reports `icon_license_notice_missing`.
A library with a module per style supplies variants. Declare them when you create the set, then add a variant for every icon in one run:

content.code:
astryx experimental icon new-set heroicons --from @heroicons/react/24/outline --variants outline,solid --default-variant outline --description 'Heroicons, outline and solid.'
astryx experimental icon add --variant solid --from @heroicons/react/24/solid --all

content.text: A library that redraws its artwork for small sizes (Heroicons' 20px mini and 16px micro) ships each of those as its own set in its own package (their export names match the 24px ones), not as variants: a variant's size comes from CSS. `--variants` lists the variants; `--default-variant` names the one each icon's own export draws (when omitted, the look a library that names its looks draws; otherwise the set's current default, else, on a set without icons, the first variant; a set with icons changes it only with `--from`, and only in a library that names its looks). `--all` adds the variant for every icon whose id an export of `--from` has (`TrashIcon` in the solid module becomes `TrashSolidIcon`, the solid variant of `trash`), and the receipt lists the icons the module has no export for. Running it again changes nothing.

A library whose icons are data (objects or SVG strings) has no components to find: create the set, declare an `adapter` in its data file (see library shapes), and run the command again; every data export then becomes an icon through the adapter. When every icon export shares a leading word, such as `feather` in `featherEye` and `featherSun`, ids and export names leave it out: `featherEye` becomes id `eye`, exported as `EyeIcon`. The prefix is read over icon-like exports only: SCREAMING_CASE constants (`README`, `VERSION`), number and boolean exports, and, next to components or icon objects, plain strings are never icons. Components named `…Provider` or `…Context` are never icons either. Leave out any other export that is not an icon with `--exclude meta,version`: the data file keeps the list in `exclude`, so a refresh leaves them out too. When a library exports one icon under several names (`Trash2` and `Trash`), the icon is recorded once and its other names become words, so `experimental icon trash-2` finds it and `experimental icon map delete trash-2` maps it. `experimental icon add` reads the prefix the same way, and reuses the icon an export already has, so its commands need no `--id`.
Every icon is a named export of your package's public entry, so apps, templates, and theme maps all import components from one place:

items: The data file's `module` is your package name or one of its package.json `exports` subpaths, never a file path. `integration check` fails otherwise.
A variant is a named look the set supplies (for example outline or solid); size comes from CSS. List the names in `variants` in the data file and the one each icon's own export draws in `default`.
Each export is named `<Name>Icon`, and a variant `<Name><Variant>Icon`, such as `TrashSolidIcon`. `experimental icon add` names them that way; `integration check` warns on another name.
Each export is a React component: a function, a class, `forwardRef` or `memo`, or what your adapter returns. `integration check` fails on a plain object or string.

It accepts SVG props (`className`, `style`, `aria-*`, `width`, `height`), draws with `currentColor`, and fills its box (`1em` or `100%`), so `<Icon icon={TrashIcon} size="sm" />` sizes and colors it like a built-in icon. The CLI cannot check this statically; the test below can.

content.text: `experimental icon add` writes the set's generated module (`generated` in the data file) and its declaration file, which re-exports each component's own types and types each adapted icon as `ComponentType<SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>>`. Add this line to your package's entry and its types; `experimental icon new-set` names the exact line and file in its receipt (see add an icon set):

content.code: export * from './icon-sets/outline/outline.generated.js';

content.text: An optional render test you can copy. Save it inside your package directory and run it there, since it imports your package by name through its `exports`, and install `react-dom` first (`npm install -D react-dom`). A library may add its own classes beside yours, so it checks the class list. A component that writes its own `width` and `height` attributes (24, from a `size` prop, say) still fills its box when it passes `style` through to its svg: the `Icon` component and `themeIcons` size the svg with CSS, which overrides size attributes. The test checks that too.
`--from` is any import specifier: a package, a package subpath, or a `./` path inside your package. Use the row that matches the library:

rows: `experimental icon add --variant solid --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --all` for every icon at once, or `experimental icon add Bin --from @acme/glyph-library/solid --id bin --variant solid` for one (the set must declare the variant: `new-set --variants`)
Every look in its export names (`XOutline24WGHT500Icon`, `XFilled24WGHT500Icon`)

`experimental icon new-set meta --from @acme/vector-icons` wraps each glyph once as `x` (`XIcon`), in the look `--default-variant` names or the library's usual default (outline, the middle weight). For another look: `experimental icon new-set meta --variants outline,filled` declares it in place, then `experimental icon add --variant filled --from @acme/vector-icons --all`
One file per icon, default export
Declare an `adapter`, then `experimental icon add Rocket --from @acme/glyph-data --definition rocket`
Declare an `adapter` that renders them, then `experimental icon add` as above

`experimental icon add Rocket --from ./src/icons/rocket.js --definition rocket`, and `--id rocket --variant solid` for its other looks. The file exports a component named as written (no library prefix is taken off), with a declaration file beside it (`rocket.d.ts`) or written in TypeScript, since the set's types re-export its own; when package.json lists `files` and none covers it, the receipt names the `files` array that publishes its folder.

content.text: An export that is not a component goes through your adapter: a function in your package that turns it into one. Declare it in the data file, `"adapter": {"module": "./src/adapt.js", "export": "adapt"}`, and `experimental icon add` writes `export const RocketIcon = adaptIcon(RocketIconSource);`:

The generated module also exports `themeIcons`: one entry per built-in definition in `map`, each an element of your own icon, hidden from assistive technology and sized `1em` by its attributes and by CSS (its `style`), so it fills the theme's icon box even when your component writes its own size attributes. The CLI rewrites it on every `experimental icon add` and `experimental icon map`, so you never write it by hand, and `integration check` proves it matches `map`. A theme uses it in one line:

`astryx integration check` reads the set without running your icons. An unmapped built-in definition is an error that names the definition's description and words and the `experimental icon map <definition> <icon id>` command that fixes it, so you or your agent can pick the icon. It names a search of your set (`experimental icon <word> --set <set>`) only when that search finds icons, and suggests one icon: the first of the suggestions `experimental icon new-set` gives for that definition. It never matches part of a word, and never writes a suggestion. Its icon-set codes:

items: `invalid_icon_set` (error): the descriptor, data file, or a definition file is invalid, for example a repeated `id`, an icon with no words, or a `map` key that is neither an Astryx definition nor one in your `definitions` folder. The set is withdrawn: apps do not see it.
`icon_builtin_definition_missing` (error): a built-in definition is not in `map`.
`icon_definition_unused` (warning): a definition you declared is not in `map`.
`icon_definition_shadowed` (warning): a definition you declared now exists in Astryx; map to Astryx's and remove yours.
`icon_module_not_public` (error), `icon_export_name` (warning), `icon_not_component` (error): the export contract above.
`icon_export_missing` (error): an export, the generated module, or the adapter does not exist.
`icon_module_invalid` (error): the set's module, a file it re-exports, or the generated module does not parse; reported once, instead of a missing export per icon.
`icon_generated_types_mismatch` (error): the generated module's declaration file is missing or does not match it.
`icon_theme_map_mismatch` (error): the theme map disagrees with the built-in entries of `map`.
`icon_source_version_drift` and `icon_license_notice_missing` (warnings): the data names another library version than the package depends on, or a set with an upstream ships no license notice.

content.text: The other Astryx definitions your set leaves unmapped are not issues: a library need not draw every definition. They are listed under "Unmapped icon definitions (optional)", and in the JSON as the validate result's `iconSets`: for each set, `unmappedDefinitions` (each `{name, description, words}`) and `suggestions` (each `{definition, icon}`, for any unmapped definition one of your icons fits). They are never counted and never fail a check.

An export fails only when the reader proves it absent; what it cannot judge it does not fail either. An icon export whose module is an `exports` target you have not built yet; an icon or adapter export it cannot prove either way (behind a re-export it cannot follow, bound to a default or namespace import, or imported from a package that is not installed); and a theme map or theme-map entry it cannot read are listed under "Not checked", and in the JSON as each set's `unchecked` (each `{icon}`, `{adapter}`, or `{entry}`, with its `reason`). Build the package, install the package it imports from, export the icon by name, or write the entry as a binding or element to have it checked. An export your built module lacks is still an error.

Errors fail the check. Warnings fail only with `--strict`. A set that maps every built-in definition and every definition it declares passes `--strict`, which integrations run in their build ({@link generic:checks}). The flow, start to finish: `experimental icon new-set` → `npm install -D typescript@6` when the receipt asks → `integration check` → `experimental icon add` (or `experimental icon map`) for each definition it lists → `integration check` passes.

items: Run `astryx integration verify` yourself before publishing. Do not put it in `prepublishOnly`: under `npm publish --dry-run` its own `npm pack` becomes a dry run too, and it checks nothing.

Declare `@astryxdesign/cli` as an optional peer (`peerDependenciesMeta`). A required peer an app cannot satisfy makes npm remove the app's CLI without a word. Icon sets are experimental, so no version range promises them, and the format may change in a patch release. A CLI reads a set only when it knows every key the set's data file uses: a key it does not know withdraws the set, naming the key. `exclude` is read only by a CLI whose data-file reference lists it ({@link schema:icon-set-data}); a set without `exclude` is read by every CLI that has `astryx experimental icon`. A CLI without it reads `experimental` as a manifest key it does not know: `astryx doctor` there warns that your package was published against a newer Astryx CLI, other commands print a one-line nudge to run it, and your icons, icon definitions, and template icon mapping do not appear ({@link generic:versioning}).

Every built-in definition needs an icon, because Core renders it. When your library has no icon with that exact meaning, map the closest one, or add your own artwork as a component file in your package (`experimental icon add <Name> --from ./src/icons/<name>.js --definition <definition>`; a ./ path is named as written). Artwork you draw is yours: note its license beside the library's, for example in a NOTICE file in the set directory.
The generated declaration file imports React types, so declare `@types/react` as an optional peer for TypeScript users.

Keep the wrapped library in `dependencies`: your generated module re-exports its components, so apps get it with your package, and `integration check` compares its range with the version the data file records.
`integration check --strict` type-checks the set's doc files; it does not type-check the generated declaration file against React's types. Run `tsc` with `@types/react` installed to check those.

Your package needs `react` (the theme map and adapter use it) as a peer, as Core does. The `experimental icon new-set` receipt names the peers your package.json does not declare yet, as the JSON to add: `react` (`>=18`), and `@types/react` and `@astryxdesign/cli` (from the release that wrote the set) as optional peers; and the `typecheck` script (`astryx integration check --strict`) when there is none.

sections.title: Share a definition with every set

content.text: Your own definitions need no change to Astryx. To share one with every set, open a pull request that copies its file into the CLI's icon definitions folder, with a description and words. Its name must not clash with another definition.

content.code:
astryx experimental icon delete              # ranked matches with import lines
astryx experimental icon outline/bin         # one icon and every variant
astryx experimental icon --list              # installed sets and their definition coverage
astryx experimental icon use outline         # make it the project's icon set

content.text: A template declares, in its descriptor's `icons`, the definition each imported icon draws (`{TrashIcon: 'delete'}`). Once the project sets `experimental.iconSet` in astryx.config (`experimental icon use` writes it), each declared icon becomes the set's icon for that definition. An icon the set does not map keeps its original import, and the copy reports every icon as mapped or kept. Nothing is guessed from names.
